provenance: Raw original125 source specifications and31-unit source map before package backend; no learner attempts. Runtime/curriculum acceptance belongs to separate root milestones. Compare typed default-aware State/Goal.

scenarios.title: Read an IPv4 address
scenarios.summary: Find the subnet boundaries and choose an unused address for a second workstation.
scenarios.objective: A workstation is configured as 192.168.10.77/27. Determine its network address, broadcast address, and usable host range, then assign a valid, different address to a second workstation.
steps: Complete the subnet assignment in the native address fields. Optional hints explain the block size and the network/host boundary.
Enter the network and broadcast addresses. Keep the same network bits when finding both boundaries.
Enter both usable endpoints and a different usable address for workstation 2. Check configuration grades all five fields.
hints: /27 leaves five host bits, so each block holds 32 addresses.
In this example the first three octets stay fixed; last-octet blocks start at multiples of 32.
Reserve the first and last addresses for network and broadcast. The second workstation must also avoid the address already in use.
scenarios.simplifications: Conventional broadcast subnets only; /31 point-to-point and /32 host routes are excluded.

guide.title: Read the prefix
guide.why: A /27 fixes 27 network bits and leaves five host bits. Each block contains 2⁵ = 32 addresses.
guide.action: Complete the subnet assignment in the native address fields. Optional hints explain the block size and the network/host boundary.

guide.title: Mark both boundaries
guide.why: The network has all host bits zero; the broadcast has all host bits one. Neither is assigned to a conventional host.
guide.action: Enter the network and broadcast addresses. Keep the same network bits when finding both boundaries.

guide.title: Identify usable hosts
guide.why: The first usable host follows the network, and the last precedes the broadcast.
guide.action: Enter both usable endpoints and a different usable address for workstation 2. Check configuration grades all five fields.

scenarios.explanation: A /27 leaves five host bits: 32 addresses per block. The block containing .77 starts at .64 and ends at .95. The network is 192.168.10.64, broadcast is 192.168.10.95, and usable hosts run from .65 through .94 (30 hosts).

address_teaching.prerequisite_note: Start here even if you have never used binary. Type addresses into the labeled fields; Check configuration checks your choices. Your original assignment and example stay separate.

concepts.title: A computer belongs to an address group
concepts.text: An IPv4 address has four numbers from 0 to 255, separated by dots. The full address identifies a computer’s interface. Its subnet is the group of addresses treated as local neighbors. The subnet mask describes that grouping; it is a rule, not another computer’s address.

concepts.title: A prefix determines the block size
concepts.text: IPv4 has 32 on/off positions, called bits. /26 keeps 26 for the network and leaves 6 host bits. Each has two choices, so 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 64 addresses per block. A larger prefix leaves fewer host bits and makes smaller blocks.

concepts.title: Find the block containing this computer
concepts.text: In this /26 example, blocks start at 0, 64, 128 and 192 in the last number. 139 is at least 128 and below the next start, 192, so it lies in 128–191. Keep the earlier numbers: the network is 192.168.5.128, broadcast is 192.168.5.191, and usable hosts are 192.168.5.129 through 192.168.5.190. The first and last addresses are reserved in this exercise.

address_teaching.example_description: Try 192.168.5.139/26 in a separate practice example. Its subnet mask is 255.255.255.192; the mask describes the grouping, while 192.168.5.139 is the computer’s address. The graded assignment uses a different address and /27. Optional prefix help explains boundaries in earlier numbers. This exercise excludes /31 and /32.
address_teaching.try_change: Fill the worked example, check it, then give Workstation 2 another free address between 129 and 190 while avoiding 139. Try 191 next and read why it cannot be assigned. The assignment remains untouched.

scenarios.title: Give each team a subnet
scenarios.summary: Divide one address pool without overlapping networks.
scenarios.objective: Allocate aligned subnets within 10.20.0.0/24 for design (60 hosts), support (28) and lab (12). Larger valid allocations are accepted if all fit without overlap.
steps: In the allocation table, give design enough addresses for 60 hosts plus network and broadcast.
Enter aligned network/prefix values for support and lab. The Hosts column lists each team’s minimum requirement.
Check work evaluates capacity, alignment, containment and overlap. Review the row results and adjust your plan.
hints: A /26 holds 62 usable hosts, /27 holds 30, and /28 holds 14.
One layout is design at .0/26, support at .64/27, lab at .96/28. Other valid layouts work.
scenarios.simplifications: No routing or DHCP modeling. Conventional subnets reserve two addresses.

guide.title: Size the largest team first
guide.why: Include two reserved addresses in every conventional subnet. Starting with the largest avoids leaving unusable fragments.
guide.action: In the allocation table, give design enough addresses for 60 hosts plus network and broadcast.

guide.title: Place the remaining teams
guide.why: Subnet boundaries must align to their block sizes. Each allocation must be inside the pool without sharing addresses.
guide.action: Enter aligned network/prefix values for support and lab. The Hosts column lists each team’s minimum requirement.

guide.title: Check the whole plan
guide.why: A plan can have sufficient capacity and still fail because two allocations overlap. More than one layout is valid.
guide.action: Check work evaluates capacity, alignment, containment and overlap. Review the row results and adjust your plan.

scenarios.explanation: 60 hosts require at least /26 (62 usable), 28 require /27 (30 usable), and 12 require /28 (14 usable). One plan is 10.20.0.0/26, 10.20.0.64/27 and 10.20.0.96/28. Other aligned, disjoint plans within the /24 are equally valid.

address_teaching.prerequisite_note: First use the subnet lesson’s network, broadcast and usable-host ideas. Here you plan several address groups inside one supplied pool. An allocation is simply one team’s chosen subnet.

concepts.title: Count all addresses, then reserve two
concepts.text: Each team needs room for its computers plus network and broadcast addresses. A /28 has 16 addresses and 14 usable hosts; a /27 has 32 addresses and 30 usable hosts. For 30 hosts, /28 is too small. Choose a block size such as 8, 16, 32 or 64 addresses—each size doubles—with enough usable places. These are powers of two.

concepts.title: Start on a real boundary
concepts.text: A block must begin at one of its own boundaries. In a /24 pool, /27 blocks begin at last numbers 0, 32, 64 and so on; /29 blocks begin at 0, 8, 16 and so on. Starting a /27 at 10 does not create a new boundary. Type its network/prefix, not an individual host address.

concepts.title: Fit distinct groups inside the pool
concepts.text: Give the largest requirement space first, then place smaller aligned blocks in unused space. Every block must stay inside the supplied pool and must not overlap another team. This is variable-length subnet masking, or VLSM: different teams can use different block sizes. Larger-than-minimum valid blocks are allowed if everything still fits.

address_teaching.example_description: In a separate 192.0.2.0/24 pool, plan for Staff 30 hosts and Visitors 6 hosts. A /27 supplies 30 usable places; a /29 supplies 6. The example table shows the chosen network/prefix for each team, and Check example verifies capacity, boundaries, containment and overlap.
address_teaching.try_change: After checking the example, move Visitors to 192.0.2.64/29 and check again: another free aligned block is valid. Then try 192.0.2.8/29 and inspect the overlap with Staff. Restore a separate block before opening the assignment.

scenarios.title: Reconnect the office client
scenarios.summary: Repair a client mask and default route.
scenarios.objective: Keep client address 192.168.40.70. Match the router LAN /26, use gateway 192.168.40.65, and reach remote server 203.0.113.10.
steps: Inspect the client’s current mask and default route.
Replace the single simulated interface address.
Update the default route, then test the remote server.
hints: A /26 here places the client and router in 192.168.40.64/26.
Use ip addr set 192.168.40.70/26 and ip route replace default via 192.168.40.65.
scenarios.simplifications: Abstract topology; no ARP, packet forwarding, latency, switches or ICMP filtering. Commands are a documented teaching subset.

guide.title: Compare the client with its router
guide.why: The LAN prefix determines which addresses are on-link. A default route must point to a router on that LAN.
guide.action: Inspect the client’s current mask and default route.

commands.explanation: Shows the client prefix and the router’s LAN prefix.
Shows the client’s default gateway.

guide.title: Correct the client prefix
guide.why: The router uses /26. The client must keep its assigned .70 address and use the same LAN prefix.
guide.action: Replace the single simulated interface address.

commands.explanation: Teaching shortcut: replaces the modeled client interface; this is not full iproute2 syntax.

guide.title: Choose the router and verify
guide.why: Remote traffic needs the reachable LAN router as its next hop. A successful ping tests this modeled path.
guide.action: Update the default route, then test the remote server.

commands.explanation: Uses the LAN router as the default next hop.
Tests reachability to the simulated remote server.

scenarios.explanation: The client .70 and router .65 share 192.168.40.64/26. Keeping .70/26 and routing remote traffic via .65 restores this modeled path. A /24 mask would incorrectly treat additional addresses as on-link.

client_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on Read an IPv4 address. Keep a workstation’s assigned address while applying the supplied LAN prefix and choosing its local router; no new subnet calculation is required here.

concepts.title: Address and prefix have different jobs
concepts.text: The address identifies this client. The prefix describes its local group. Follow the supplied LAN plan while keeping the client’s assigned address; changing the gateway does not change that address.

concepts.title: A default gateway is the next hop
concepts.text: For a destination outside the local group, this task uses the supplied LAN router as its default next hop. The remote target is a different address reached through that router, not the value to enter as the gateway.

concepts.title: Apply, then inspect
concepts.text: Fields are saved drafts until Apply client settings changes this virtual client. The diagram shows applied values. ip addr and ip route give compact simulated views; the router’s plan is supplied context, not information a real ip addr command discovers. The retained ip addr set form is an older simulator editor shortcut, not full Linux syntax.

concepts.title: Test the local and remote paths separately
concepts.text: A reply from the LAN router does not prove the required remote setup is correct. Try ping with the supplied router and target addresses, then Check work for all three requirements. These are abstract path checks, without ARP, packet forwarding or real ICMP.

client_teaching.example_description: A different client is assigned 198.51.100.150. Its supplied LAN router is 198.51.100.129/27 and remote target is 203.0.113.90. Repair the current /24 prefix and .1 gateway without changing .150. Practice is separate from the office assignment.

example_actions.title: Inspect the client
example_actions.explanation: Read the current address/prefix alongside the supplied router LAN plan. This query changes no settings.

command.explanation: Compact simulated client view; not a complete real iproute2 dump.

example_actions.title: Inspect the default route
example_actions.explanation: Compare the current next hop with the supplied router. This query changes no settings.

command.explanation: Shows the one modeled default gateway.

example_actions.title: Apply the example LAN plan
example_actions.explanation: Insert fills the three example fields only: keep .150, use /27 and choose .129 as gateway. Press Apply client settings to apply them to the example.

example_actions.title: Test the remote target
example_actions.explanation: Run this path check after applying the example settings. A simulated reply checks this particular target, not full network or application behavior.

command.explanation: Checks the abstract remote path in this example; no real packet or host command runs.

client_teaching.try_change: After the example passes, change only Default gateway to 198.51.100.130 and Apply. ping 198.51.100.129 can still reply locally, but ping 203.0.113.90 is unreachable. Check example shows the route still needs work. Restore gateway .129 and Apply to repair the example.

scenarios.title: Share a report safely
scenarios.summary: Give Alex read/write access while keeping the file private.
scenarios.objective: Let alex read and write /srv/report.txt; give other users no permissions on that file.
steps: Compare the file’s ownership and permissions with alex’s groups.
Change the file mode. An ownership-based solution can also work.
Inspect the repaired mode, then optionally use the simulator’s access probe.
hints: alex belongs to editors. Group bits need read (4) plus write (2).
chmod 660 /srv/report.txt gives owner/group read-write and no other permissions.
scenarios.simplifications: Administrator mutations; test-access uses ordinary POSIX owner/group/other precedence. No ACLs, root override, special mode bits or SELinux. Privacy excludes the root administrator; all other modeled users and the other permission class are checked. Group access is valid only while no other modeled user can use it.

guide.title: Read owner and group access
guide.why: POSIX chooses one permission class: owner first, then a matching group, otherwise other.
guide.action: Compare the file’s ownership and permissions with alex’s groups.

commands.explanation: Reads the symbolic mode, owner and group columns.
Shows primary and supplementary group memberships.

guide.title: Give Alex the required access
guide.why: Alex belongs to editors. Group read/write works here only while no other modeled non-administrator user can use that access. Changing ownership to Alex and removing group permissions is another valid solution.
guide.action: Change the file mode. An ownership-based solution can also work.

commands.explanation: Gives owner and group read/write; leaves other users no file permissions.

guide.title: Verify effective access
guide.why: Correct file bits alone are insufficient if a parent directory cannot be traversed.
guide.action: Inspect the repaired mode, then optionally use the simulator’s access probe.

commands.explanation: Confirms the resulting permission bits.
Simulator-only probe of alex’s effective access through the full path.

scenarios.explanation: With root as owner and editors as group, mode 660 gives alex group read/write and removes all other-class permissions. Changing ownership to alex while retaining restrictive bits is another valid solution. Owner permissions take precedence over group permissions.

legacy_access_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use the inspect-and-repair method from Access policy and safe file changes. This older exercise gives you a virtual administrator role; it does not operate on your computer.

concepts.title: Choose one permission class
concepts.text: Every entry has an owner and a group. ls -l /srv/brief.txt shows its owner, group and read/write/execute bits. The model chooses owner bits when the user owns the entry; otherwise matching group bits; otherwise other bits. These classes are not added together. id dana shows Dana belongs to reviewers.

concepts.title: Translate the requested access
concepts.text: Read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1 in an octal mode digit. On the practice file, chmod 660 /srv/brief.txt gives owner and reviewers read/write and gives the other class no bits. Dana uses group bits while root owns it. Changing ownership to Dana and using 600 is another possible method; neither an exact mode nor one repair order is a hidden goal.

concepts.title: Verify the user, not only the listing
concepts.text: test-access dana /srv/brief.txt rw is a simulator-only probe, not a Linux utility. It checks parent search permission and file access for Dana. Here mutations are administrative even when an ordinary user could not change the file. Privacy excludes the root administrator but also checks other modeled people: the unrelated observer must not gain access.

concepts.title: Know this small terminal
concepts.text: Type one explained command and choose Run or Enter. Insert action fills the input only. This older terminal uses exact absolute paths and whitespace tokens, without shell quoting or expansion. It has no ACL, special mode bits or root access override. Practice remains separate; later Check work grades the full assignment from its current access state.

legacy_access_teaching.example_description: Give dana read/write access to /srv/brief.txt, keeping the file private from the other class and every modeled nonadministrator except Dana. root owns it and reviewers is its group; Dana already belongs to reviewers. Inspect, change and probe this separate example.

commands.explanation: Read the compact mode, owner and group columns before changing anything.
Read the modeled primary and supplementary groups; displayed numeric IDs are derived labels, not account-management records.
Give owner and reviewers read/write while removing other-class bits.
Probe Dana's effective read/write access in this simulator.
The unrelated observer should remain denied in this simulator.

legacy_access_teaching.try_change: After success, run chmod 440 /srv/brief.txt and probe Dana for rw. Removing write makes the current access check fail. Restore 660 for the group-based method, then probe and Check example again.

scenarios.title: Unlock the project directory
scenarios.summary: Trace group access through a directory tree.
scenarios.objective: Give blair read access to /srv/project/notes.txt without public file permissions. Repair group membership and traversal as needed.
steps: Inspect both blair’s groups and each component of the file path.
Add editors without replacing existing groups. This model refreshes sessions immediately.
Give editors directory traversal, then verify access to the file.
hints: Directory read lists names; execute allows traversal. Both can be useful, but traversal is necessary here.
usermod -aG editors blair followed by chmod 750 /srv/project repairs this path.
scenarios.simplifications: No supplementary-group session refresh, ACLs or SELinux. Alternative ownership/permission repairs are accepted if effective access and privacy hold.

guide.title: Trace the entire path
guide.why: Reading a file requires search/execute on every parent directory, plus read on the file.
guide.action: Inspect both blair’s groups and each component of the file path.

commands.explanation: Checks whether blair belongs to the file’s group.
Shows the modeled owner, group and mode at every path component.

guide.title: Add the missing group
guide.why: Supplementary group membership allows the group permission class to apply.
guide.action: Add editors without replacing existing groups. This model refreshes sessions immediately.

commands.explanation: Appends editors to blair’s supplementary groups.

guide.title: Restore directory traversal
guide.why: Directory read lists names; directory execute permits access through the directory.
guide.action: Give editors directory traversal, then verify access to the file.

commands.explanation: Gives the editors group read and search on the project directory.
Simulator-only effective read-access probe.

scenarios.explanation: Adding blair to editors permits the group class to apply. Mode 750 on /srv/project adds the execute/search bit missing from 740. The file’s existing group-read bit then becomes reachable through all parent directories. Effective-access alternatives are accepted.

legacy_access_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use Share a report safely to choose owner/group/other permissions. This independent example adds a path with more than one directory. It keeps its own users, modes and command history.

concepts.title: Every parent needs search
concepts.text: Reading a known file needs search/execute on every directory leading to it, including /, then read permission on the file. Directory read lists names; search lets a user pass through a known path. Missing search can block a readable file. Here namei /srv/review/plan.txt gives a compact simulated octal-mode/owner/group view, not the full real namei output.

concepts.title: Membership and bits are separate
concepts.text: id evan initially lacks inspectors. usermod -aG inspectors evan appends one existing group and keeps Evan's primary group. This administrative simulation refreshes membership immediately; real existing login sessions may need refreshing. It does not create accounts/groups or model credentials. All group names must already exist in the supplied membership lists.

concepts.title: Add only what access needs
concepts.text: The directory starts 740: group read without search. After adding inspectors, chmod 710 /srv/review gives the group search without requiring listing or write. The existing 640 file then supplies group read. 750 also works; exact directory read/write bits are not requested. Inspections are administrative; use test-access to ask about Evan's effective access.

concepts.title: Public is not the same as exclusive
concepts.text: This task removes the file's other-class permissions; it does not ban an existing teammate who belongs to inspectors. test-access evan /srv/review/plan.txt r is a simulator-only check. In the full assignment Blair must gain read access without public file bits; existing Alex/editor access can remain. Current effective access, not a membership-change history, is graded.

legacy_access_teaching.example_description: Let evan read /srv/review/plan.txt without public file permissions. Add the existing inspectors group and repair parent search as needed. The existing colleague may retain access. This example is independent of Blair's project assignment.

commands.explanation: Inspect the current group list before changing it.
Inspect compact simulated path components; this is not a full namei output/options model.
Append the known group; simulated sessions update immediately.
Give inspectors search on the directory. Listing and write are not required here.
Simulator-only probe of Evan's read access through all parents.

legacy_access_teaching.try_change: After success, run chmod 700 /srv/review. The file still has group-read bits, but Evan loses parent search. Probe r and Check example, then restore 710 (or 750) and verify the path again.

scenarios.title: Find the failing requests
scenarios.summary: Locate a log and extract the relevant lines.
scenarios.objective: Find app.log under /var/log, then produce exactly its ERROR lines as the last text query.

files./var/log/app.log:
09:00 INFO startup ready
09:02 ERROR database unavailable
09:03 INFO retry scheduled
09:04 ERROR request timeout
09:05 WARN queue growing

steps: Produce both ERROR lines as the last text query. A later unfiltered query will change the graded result.
hints: grep takes a one-word literal and a path; pipelines can also filter cat output.
grep ERROR /var/log/app.log produces both requested lines.
scenarios.simplifications: Literal case-sensitive matching only; no regex, globbing, quoting, redirection or general shell. find only searches the simulated log map.

guide.title: Locate the log
guide.why: Finding the correct file prevents filtering unrelated messages. All paths here belong to the simulated filesystem.
guide.action: Locate app.log under /var/log.

commands.explanation: Searches the simulated log catalog for that file name.

guide.title: Read before filtering
guide.why: Inspect the message format to choose a literal that isolates the requested severity.
guide.action: Read the application log.

commands.explanation: Prints the modeled log, including INFO, WARN and ERROR lines.

guide.title: Extract just the errors
guide.why: grep retains matching lines. This documented subset matches a case-sensitive one-word literal.
guide.action: Produce both ERROR lines as the last text query. A later unfiltered query will change the graded result.

commands.explanation: Prints only the lines containing ERROR.
An alternate pipeline that produces the same result.

scenarios.explanation: Both ERROR lines must be retained and the INFO/WARN lines excluded. Direct grep or cat piped into grep produces the same resulting text. The most recent successful text query is graded, so printing the unfiltered log afterward removes current completion.

legacy_logs_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use the inspect-then-change method from Files, paths and safe handovers. This older log exercise has a small fixed catalog; its find and filter forms are simpler than the later recursive-search and script units.

concepts.title: Locate and inspect the supplied text
concepts.text: A log is a sequence of text lines describing events. find /var/log -name worker.log locates that exact basename in this supplied catalog. It does not use wildcard patterns, depth or directory permissions. cat /var/log/worker.log displays the whole log. All paths are virtual; no host log is read.

concepts.title: Filter a literal substring
concepts.text: grep FAIL /var/log/worker.log keeps each line containing the case-sensitive text FAIL. This exercise treats one word literally, not as a regular expression or a severity-field parser. FAIL and fail differ. There are two requested FAIL lines and INFO/WARN lines to exclude. The separate audit log has different messages; inspect the right source.

concepts.title: Pass text through a pipeline
concepts.text: cat /var/log/worker.log | grep FAIL produces the same selected text. A pipe passes one stage's output to the next. Put spaces around | in this small terminal. There is no shell quoting, expansion, redirection or general command evaluator. tail -n 3 /var/log/worker.log inspects recent lines but can omit an earlier failure; filtering the full log avoids that omission.

concepts.title: The current selection is the task
concepts.text: Successful cat, grep and tail queries replace the selected result. After a correct filter, printing the whole log makes the result too broad; filter again to repair. find, show and help only inspect and leave it alone. Check example reads the current selected text, not command history. A no-match query displays a message and selects empty text; no grep exit-status model is taught here.

legacy_logs_teaching.example_description: Locate worker.log and select exactly its two FAIL lines. Keep their original order and exclude INFO/WARN messages and the unrelated audit log. This practice uses different files/messages/needle from the app.log/ERROR assignment.

files./var/log/worker.log:
11:00 INFO worker ready
11:01 FAIL task18 rejected
11:02 INFO retry queued
11:03 FAIL task27 expired
11:04 WARN queue growing
files./var/log/audit-practice.log:
11:00 INFO audit opened
11:05 FAIL unrelated audit warning

commands.explanation: Find the exact supplied basename; this fixed catalog form is not a recursive Tree search.
Read every line before deciding what to select.
Inspect recent messages; this omits an earlier FAIL, so refilter the full log afterward.
Select the two lines containing the literal uppercase FAIL.
An equivalent spaced pipeline; no extra command history is required.

legacy_logs_teaching.try_change: After success, run cat /var/log/worker.log and Check example. The selected text now includes INFO/WARN, so the current task fails. Repair with grep FAIL /var/log/worker.log (or the explained pipeline), then check again.

scenarios.title: Bring the service back
scenarios.summary: Repair a bad configuration and restore startup behavior.
scenarios.objective: Repair atlas to listen on port 8080, start it with that configuration, and enable it for boot.
steps: Inspect the unit and its journal. A legacy saved attempt may have no journal history; try starting it to record a diagnostic.
In the simulated /etc/atlas.conf editor, replace eighty with 8080 and choose Save configuration. The editor changes only this attempt.
Run each command separately and compare active with enabled.
hints: The saved port is a word. Use the simulated config editor to save a numeric port; running and enabled are separate.
Save 8080 in the editor, then restart atlas and enable it for boot.
scenarios.simplifications: Single modeled service, one configuration key. No unit dependency graph, privileges, socket binding, processes or actual boot.

guide.title: Inspect the failed start
guide.why: Status describes the unit; the journal explains recorded start failures. Enabling at boot and running now are independent.
guide.action: Inspect the unit and its journal. A legacy saved attempt may have no journal history; try starting it to record a diagnostic.

commands.explanation: Shows Loaded, Active and runtime information for the modeled unit.
Reads modeled unit events using journal-style output.

guide.title: Repair the saved configuration
guide.why: The port must be an integer from 1 through 65535. Saving a file does not reload a running service.
guide.action: In the simulated /etc/atlas.conf editor, replace eighty with 8080 and choose Save configuration. The editor changes only this attempt.

guide.title: Restart, enable, then verify
guide.why: Restart applies the saved port. Enable configures future boot startup but does not start the service.
guide.action: Run each command separately and compare active with enabled.

commands.explanation: Starts the service using the saved configuration.
Enables the unit for boot.
Checks whether it is running now.
Checks whether it is enabled for boot.

scenarios.explanation: The original word eighty is not a valid numeric port. Saving port=8080 repairs the file; restart loads that value into the running service. Enable is independent and makes the unit start at boot. A saved config edit alone does not change the currently loaded port.

service_teaching.prerequisite_note: No service-management experience is needed. Read this introduction or open the full assignment. The example keeps its own saved configuration, running service and command history.

concepts.title: A service works in the background
concepts.text: A service is a program that can keep working without an open terminal. This lab models a fictional service called atlas. Its configuration file holds a port number: a numbered entry point for an application. Here it is only a simulated value; no real program or socket is started.

concepts.title: Look for evidence before changing anything
concepts.text: systemctl status atlas reports whether atlas is running now and enabled for future boot. journalctl -u atlas reads recorded events for that service. A failed start can leave an explanation in the journal. Type one command in the terminal and press Enter or Run; its output appears above the input.

concepts.title: A saved file and a running program are different
concepts.text: Use the Port field in the simulated /etc/atlas.conf editor and choose Save configuration. The port must be a number from 1 to 65535 for atlas to start. Saving alone does not change a running service. Restart stops and starts atlas with the saved value; start does not reload a service that is already running.

concepts.title: Running now or starting with the computer
concepts.text: Enable records that a service should start when the computer starts (at boot); it does not start the service now. Restart or start controls whether it runs now. Verify both: is-active reports active when running, while is-enabled reports enabled for boot. In this lab, check both after repairing the configuration.

service_teaching.example_description: Try repairing a separate practice copy of atlas to use port 9090. Inspect its failed status and journal, put 9090 in the example editor, save, restart and enable it. Then verify both states. Use example port fills only the editor draft; it does not save or run anything.

commands.explanation: Inspect current activity and boot enablement before editing.
Read the saved diagnostic from the failed start.
Read the saved configuration; an unsaved editor draft is not this file.
Stop and start atlas using its saved configuration.
Enable future boot startup; this does not start atlas.
See whether atlas is running now.
See whether atlas is set to start when the computer starts.

service_teaching.try_change: After verifying the example, save port 9091 without restarting and inspect status: the running instance still uses 9090. Restart to load 9091, then check why it fails this example’s required port. Restore 9090 and restart. Finally try systemctl disable atlas: it can keep running while disabled for boot.

scenarios.title: Repair the internal DNS answer
scenarios.summary: Correct a record and reload the authoritative zone.
scenarios.objective: Make portal.lab.test resolve to 192.0.2.80 in the loaded authoritative zone.
steps: Read the zone and query the current answer.

concepts.title: A name and its A record
concepts.text: An A record associates a supplied host name with an IPv4 address. Here the authoritative answer is the value held by the serving copy of this one-record zone. There is no recursive lookup or cache.

concepts.title: Saved is not yet serving

concepts.title: A larger serial before reload

concepts.title: Volume, device and mountpoint
concepts.text: A volume is the supplied block of simulated storage. Its known device identifies it; /data is the place where it is mounted. This example never opens a real device or changes your computer.

concepts.title: Used capacity versus disposable cache
concepts.text: df -h reports the total and used MiB. du -sh /data/cache reports the only explicitly disposable data here. Removing 450 MiB from 1850 leaves 1400/2000 MiB, or 70%; the objective accepts usage at most 80%.

concepts.title: Saved pointer versus current mount
concepts.text: Save configuration edits only the simulated /etc/fstab pointer. It does not mount the volume or make it writable. Read cat /etc/fstab to compare that saved pointer with the supplied known device.

concepts.title: Cleanup needs read-write access

concepts.title: Verify the saved entry and current state
concepts.text: umount /data makes the current volume unavailable. mount /data uses the saved device and restores read-write access if it is correct. This cycle is useful verification, not required to pass; the assignment is checked from its current state.

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: Quoted expansions preserve spaces and empty data. printf treats percent signs in a %s argument as ordinary data, not a new format.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases

printf 'Site: %s\nTask: %s\n' "$site" "$TASK"
hints: The lab supplies SITE and TASK. Read their values as "$SITE" and "$TASK"; create your own named value with name=value if useful.
Double quotes keep each expanded value together. printf separates the fixed format from the data.
A format such as printf 'Site: %s\n' "$SITE" prints one complete line.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Start here: no shell knowledge is needed.

concepts.title: A script is a saved set of instructions
concepts.text: Type instructions in the script editor. Run reads them from top to bottom and shows what they print. Here it runs only in the offline simulator; it cannot change your computer.

concepts.title: Comments and printed text
concepts.text: A line starting with # is a comment: a note that is not run. printf prints text. A command name comes first, followed by the information it needs, separated by spaces.

concepts.title: Variables are names for values
concepts.text: visitor='Mina' creates a variable named visitor; use no spaces around =. "$visitor" reads its value. The example also has ROOM, supplied by the lab before Run. You create visitor; you do not create ROOM. In the assignment, SITE and TASK are supplied instead.

concepts.title: Quotes and printf formatting
concepts.text: Single quotes keep the format text literal. In double quotes, $visitor is replaced by its value and kept together, even with spaces. In printf, %s means “insert the next text value here”; \n (backslash then n) means “start a new line.” The format and the values are separate pieces.

teaching.example:
# A comment is a note, not an instruction.
visitor='Mina'
printf 'Welcome\n'
printf 'Hello, %s!\n' "$visitor"
printf 'Room: %s\n' "$ROOM"

scenarios.title: Reject a missing destination
scenarios.summary: Use a condition and exit status to make failure visible.
scenarios.objective: If argument 1 is empty or missing, print Destination required to standard error and exit 2. Otherwise print Destination: VALUE to standard output and exit 0. Do not change files.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Each test starts with its own sample inputs. Simulated files reset before each test. Inspect the inputs and expected results.
guide.action: Use the case selector to inspect inputs, then edit the script.

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: Shell conditions inspect exit status: zero means true/success. A guard gives a useful diagnostic on standard error and stops before normal output. Keeping errors separate helps callers.
guide.action: Run script executes every case. Inspect the output and specific failing check, edit, and retry.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases
guide.why: A script that works once can still fail on spaces, missing files or empty data.
guide.action: Compare the cases. Why does the same script handle every input?

scenarios.explanation:
Shell conditions inspect exit status: zero means true/success. A guard gives a useful diagnostic on standard error and stops before normal output. Keeping errors separate helps callers.

One supported solution:
if [ -z "$1" ]; then
    printf 'Destination required\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
printf 'Destination: %s\n' "$1"
hints: [ -z "$1" ] succeeds when the first argument is empty. Spaces around [ and ] matter.
An if runs its then block when the condition returns status 0.
>&2 sends the message to standard error. exit 2 ends the script with a deliberate failure status.

concepts.title: Commands report whether they succeeded
concepts.text: An exit status is a number a command returns: 0 means success; other numbers report another outcome. The script normally returns its last command’s status. exit 2 stops it immediately and returns 2.

concepts.title: Choose what runs with a condition
concepts.text: [ -z "$1" ] tests whether argument 1 is empty or missing. -n tests the opposite: whether text is non-empty. Keep spaces after [ and before ]. if runs the then instructions when the test succeeds (status 0); else gives another path. fi ends the choice. A ; can separate instructions where a new line would also work.

concepts.title: Keep problems separate from normal output
concepts.text: Standard error is a second output channel for problem messages. >&2 sends a printf message there instead of to normal output. A guard is an early check that explains a problem and stops before doing other work.

teaching.example:
if [ -z "$1" ]; then
    printf 'Name needed\n' >&2
    exit 2
else
    printf 'Hello, %s\n' "$1"
fi
teaching.inputs: No arguments are supplied, so the example takes the missing-name path. The message belongs in Standard error.
teaching.try_change: Change -z to -n, which tests for a non-empty value. Run again with the same empty input and observe the other path.

guide.title: Understand the task

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: Sole quoted "$@" expands to one word per positional argument. With no arguments it supplies zero words, so the loop runs zero times. This prevents spaces in names becoming extra iterations.
guide.action: Run script executes every case. Inspect the output and specific failing check, edit, and retry.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases

guide.action: Compare the cases. Why does the same script handle every input?

scenarios.explanation:
Sole quoted "$@" expands to one word per positional argument. With no arguments it supplies zero words, so the loop runs zero times. This prevents spaces in names becoming extra iterations.

One supported solution:
for file in "$@"; do
    printf 'File: %s\n' "$file"
    cat "$file"
done
hints: for file in "$@" iterates over the original argument boundaries.
Inside the loop, quote "$file" for both the heading and cat.
Keep the print and cat inside do … done so each heading stays next to its contents.

concepts.title: Repeat a group of instructions

concepts.title: Repeat while an action succeeds

concepts.title: End-of-input is a status, not always an empty value
concepts.text: read reports a nonzero status when it reaches the end before a newline. It can still have stored useful final text in the variable. A complete blank line is different: read succeeds and stores an empty value.

concepts.title: Try another condition after failure
concepts.text: A || B runs B only if A fails. The example accepts either a complete read or a non-empty final value. Once both fail, the loop ends; with no input it does no work.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on function calls and the earlier batch failure flag. This lesson distinguishes return from exit.

concepts.title: Return ends this call; exit ends the script
concepts.text: A helper can reject one item without stopping the whole batch. return 1 leaves the function and gives the caller status 1. exit 1 ends the complete script, so later items never get a chance.

concepts.title: The caller decides how to continue
concepts.text: An if can call a function as its condition. Status 0 chooses then; nonzero chooses else. The caller can remember a failure and continue. return without a number uses the previous command’s status.

concepts.title: Batch status remembers earlier problems
concepts.text: A later successful item must not erase an earlier rejection. The shared failure flag records whether any item failed. The no-op : is a successful command for an intentionally empty branch.

        printf 'Name needed\n' >&2

    printf 'Welcome: %s\n' "$1"

printf 'Still running\n'
admit Mina

concepts.title: Arguments can play different roles

concepts.title: Shift removes leading positional arguments
concepts.text: shift removes the current $1: the old $2 becomes $1 and $# decreases by one. shift 2 removes two; shift 0 changes nothing. A count larger than the number of arguments fails with status 1 and leaves them unchanged in this Bash reference subset.

concepts.title: Preserve each remaining item
concepts.text: After consuming the header, "$@" still keeps every remaining argument separate, including a value containing spaces or an empty value. Inside a function, shift affects that function’s arguments; its caller’s arguments return unchanged when the function finishes.

concepts.title: Read the access groups
concepts.text: ls -l shows permissions in three groups: owner, group and everyone else. r means read, w means write and x means search/enter for a directory (execute for a file). A dash means that permission is absent. Alex owns these practice files.

concepts.title: Understand the numbers
concepts.text: Octal permissions combine read=4, write=2 and execute/search=1. Thus 700 gives the owner all three permissions and nobody else any; 600 gives only owner read+write. ls -ld PATH inspects the directory itself rather than its contents.

concepts.title: Choose safer creation defaults
concepts.text: umask blocks permissions on NEW entries; it does not edit existing ones. umask 077 blocks group and everyone-else access. Normal new directories start from 777, giving 700; touch creates ordinary files from 666, giving 600. touch also updates an existing entry’s time without emptying it.

A blank, malformed, wrong-prefix, duplicate or reserved choice has a different cause. Read the feedback and retry; many different valid addresses pass.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: IPv4 foundations are useful preparation, but this introduction explains the IPv6 notation needed here. No binary calculation or router command setup is required.

concepts.title: Read an IPv6 address
concepts.text: IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits, written as eight groups separated by colons. Each group has up to four hexadecimal digits: 0–9, then a–f for values ten–fifteen. Leading zeros in a group may be omitted. One :: can stand for enough all-zero groups to make eight groups; it may appear only once.

concepts.title: Keep the subnet part
concepts.text: In these /64 examples, the first four full groups identify the subnet and the final four identify the interface. fd71:55:44::20 expands to fd71:0055:0044:0000:0000:0000:0000:0020. Keep the first half and choose a different ordinary workstation part.

concepts.title: Use the workspace
concepts.text: Select NewPC, keep Addresses & interfaces selected, and type the full address/prefix in its field. Check applies all edited fields and tests the current result. Devices on the same link can talk directly; no default route is needed for this assignment. This manual editor includes a connected/on-link prefix by default; router advertisements are not being simulated.

concepts.title: Choose an ordinary unique address
concepts.text: Each interface on this link needs a different address. IPv6 has no broadcast address: do not subtract an IPv4-style broadcast from its range. The all-zero interface identifier and a small reserved subnet-anycast range are not ordinary workstation choices here; the checker explains these cases.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: ExistingPC uses fd71:55:44::10/64. Give NewPC fd71:55:44::20/64. Load example settings fills the practice fields only; Apply and test example uses them. You can also type the address yourself.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: Change NewPC to fd71:55:44::37/64, then apply and test again. ExistingPC must keep its original address.

scenarios.title: Repair an IPv6 workstation’s path
scenarios.summary: Distinguish a wrong local prefix from an unreachable default next hop.
scenarios.objective: Client must remain 2001:db8:10::10/64. Restore its path to Server at 2001:db8:20::20 and to R1’s office address 2001:db8:10::1. Repair Client’s prefix/default route, keep all supplied interface addresses/prefixes on other devices, and verify replies as well as requests.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Distinguish a wrong local prefix from an unreachable default next hop.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Check whether Client’s connected prefix wrongly includes the server’s network. Then inspect its default next hop.
guide.action: Use Addresses & interfaces for Client’s /64, then Static routes for ::/0 through the actual office router on lan.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: The /64 keeps only the office subnet local. The server therefore uses the default route. Its next hop must be R1 on the office link; an unassigned fe80::99 cannot resolve. R1 forwards to the server network, and the server’s default route provides the reply. Repairing only one fault is partial work.
hints: Check whether Client’s connected prefix wrongly includes the server’s network. Then inspect its default next hop.
Use Addresses & interfaces for Client’s /64, then Static routes for ::/0 through the actual office router on lan.
A valid global on-link address for the same router can also work. What matters is a reachable neighboring router and correct current paths.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on the first IPv6 assignment and the earlier idea of a default gateway. Link-local addresses are introduced here; they do not need a global subnet match.

concepts.title: Decide local or remote
concepts.text: The manually connected prefix tells this model which addresses are local. A mistaken /32 can make a remote destination look local, so the workstation searches the wrong link instead of using its router. Keep the supplied address and repair its /64.

concepts.title: Choose a default router
concepts.text: The route ::/0 is the least-specific default: it catches destinations that do not match a more-specific route. Its next hop is the neighboring router, not the remote server. Here fe80::1 is the router’s link-local address on Client’s lan; the outgoing interface scopes that address to this link.

concepts.title: Edit routes natively
concepts.text: Select Client, then Static routes to edit its default row. Keep destination ::/0, set next hop fe80::1, outgoing interface lan and a usable distance such as 1. Check configuration applies address and route edits together. Inspect applied forwarding paths shows why a request or reply failed. Distance is a preference number used between equally specific active routes; lower is preferred. Leave 1 here.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: Repair Client’s prefix to /64 without changing its fd71:55:10::10 address, then use the office router fe80::1 as its default next hop on lan. The remote server is fd71:55:20::20.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: After the example works, change only the default next hop to fe80::88 and test. Restore fe80::1 and retry.

scenarios.title: Put a link-local next hop on the right link
scenarios.summary: Repair a route’s outgoing interface across a router transit link.
scenarios.objective: R1’s route toward 2001:db8:20::/64 uses R2’s link-local next hop fe80::2, but it points at the wrong outgoing interface. Restore Client’s access to R2’s branch address 2001:db8:20::1 and Server at 2001:db8:20::20, including replies. Keep supplied address/prefix settings, including unnumbered transit interfaces; keep R1 forwarding enabled.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Repair a route’s outgoing interface across a router transit link.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Look at the link labels in the topology. R2’s fe80::2 is on transit, not on the office link.
guide.action: Select R1 → Static routes. Pair the neighboring next hop with the interface that actually reaches that neighbor.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: A link-local next hop has meaning only on its chosen outgoing link. Moving the route to transit makes R2 the resolved neighbor. R2’s connected branch prefix and office return route complete both directions. A full route or supported equivalent host routes for both required destinations can meet the outcome.
hints: Look at the link labels in the topology. R2’s fe80::2 is on transit, not on the office link.
Select R1 → Static routes. Pair the neighboring next hop with the interface that actually reaches that neighbor.
The server itself is not directly on the transit link. R2 must receive and forward the traffic, with a return path through R1.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on local versus remote destinations and a default next hop. This assignment adds a router-to-router transit link and explicit scope.

concepts.title: Link-local means this link
concepts.text: A fe80:: address identifies an interface on one link. It is not forwarded to another link, and the same text may be used on different links. A static route with a link-local next hop therefore needs the correct outgoing interface as well as the address.

concepts.title: Forward to a neighbor, not straight to the remote host
concepts.text: The transit link has link-local addresses only in this model. R1 sends the packet to R2’s transit interface; R2 then forwards it onto the branch network. A directly-on-link route would wrongly search the transit link for the remote server.

concepts.title: Keep both directions
concepts.text: R2 already has the office return route. Keep the supplied address settings and forwarding state; repair R1’s route interface and verify both the branch router and server. This models forwarding decisions, not Neighbor Discovery packet exchange.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: On R1, the route to fd71:55:20::/64 uses neighboring R2 at fe80::2. Select Static routes and choose the transit outgoing interface; the office interface is the wrong link.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: Change R1’s outgoing interface back to office and test the failure, then restore transit. Inspect the selected first hop.

scenarios.title: Find the route that overrides a working default
scenarios.summary: Diagnose why one destination fails while another still works.
scenarios.objective: Client can reach Monitor at 2001:db8:30::30 but cannot reach Server at 2001:db8:20::20. Investigate Client’s static routes and restore both request/reply paths without changing supplied interface addresses/prefixes. Remove an unnecessary faulty route or repair it; valid alternate routing outcomes are accepted.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Diagnose why one destination fails while another still works.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Compare both destinations with the route prefixes. A working default does not guarantee it is selected for every destination.
guide.action: The /64 row wins over ::/0 regardless of their distances. Inspect the next hop of the more-specific route.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: The server matches the narrow /64, so its higher distance does not make the default win. The unassigned next hop fails neighbor resolution. Removing the unnecessary narrow route lets the default handle both destinations; repairing it also works. Merely changing its distance to another installed value leaves the same mistake.
hints: Compare both destinations with the route prefixes. A working default does not guarantee it is selected for every destination.
The /64 row wins over ::/0 regardless of their distances. Inspect the next hop of the more-specific route.
Repairing the /64 next hop or removing that row can both work. Keep monitoring access as part of your verification.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on static route fields and next-hop reachability. This lesson introduces longest-prefix selection before distance.

concepts.title: Specific destinations win first
concepts.text: A router or workstation chooses the matching route with the longest prefix. Only equally specific active routes compare distance. A /64 route therefore beats ::/0 even when its distance is 200 and the default’s is 1.

concepts.title: Fix the misleading row
concepts.text: A route can be installed yet fail to reach its next hop. Increasing its distance does not make a shorter prefix win. Remove an unnecessary bad row, or repair its next hop/interface. Confirm the other service still works afterward.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: Client’s ::/0 route through fe80::1 works for the monitor, but a fd71:55:20::/64 row through fe80::99 breaks the server path. Remove that bad row, or repair its next hop.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: Instead of removing the narrow row, keep its /64 and distance 200 but set its next hop to fe80::1. Both required paths should still work.

scenarios.title: Make the backup route work before the outage
scenarios.summary: Repair a floating default and verify normal and failed-link behavior.
scenarios.objective: Client must prefer its primary interface to reach Server at 2001:db8:20::20, switch to backup when primary is unavailable, and retain primary when backup is unavailable. Repair its default routes and preserve all supplied interface addresses/prefixes. Keep the saved base interfaces up. Check runs three separate simulated conditions and verifies replies and the first outgoing interface; equivalent usable distance pairs are accepted.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Repair a floating default and verify normal and failed-link behavior.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Normal reachability alone does not exercise the backup next hop. Read all three condition results.
guide.action: Select Client → Static routes. The backup next hop must resolve on backup, and its route must remain less preferred than primary.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: With equally specific defaults, primary wins by lower distance. When primary is down its row is inactive; backup must resolve its own neighboring router and carry both directions. The checker uses clones for failures and checks the actual first hop, so one happy-path ping, reversed preference or a single permanent route does not pass.
hints: Normal reachability alone does not exercise the backup next hop. Read all three condition results.
Select Client → Static routes. The backup next hop must resolve on backup, and its route must remain less preferred than primary.
Different unequal distances can be valid. Reversing preference or disabling a base interface cannot substitute for a working normal-and-failure configuration.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on longest-prefix and route distance. This lesson adds simulated link failures and checks which route is preferred.

concepts.title: Prefer one route, retain another
concepts.text: Two equally specific routes can use different distances. The lower distance is preferred while its interface is up. A higher-distance route is a floating backup; it becomes useful when the preferred route is no longer active. This model does not infer link failure from a silent neighbor timeout.

concepts.title: Test the backup before relying on it
concepts.text: Normal success can hide a broken backup. The checker tests the current configuration, then a copy with primary down and another with backup down. The saved base state is not changed. The first interface must match the requested preference in each case.

concepts.title: Keep a usable pair
concepts.text: Use distinct distances, usable next-hop neighbors and the correct outgoing interfaces. Equal-cost choices are explicitly unsupported in this first static model. No particular pair of numeric distances is required if preference and failure behavior are correct.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: Client has two office links. Keep the primary default preferred and repair the backup default’s next hop to fe80::1 on backup. Apply tests normal operation and each single-interface failure using separate simulated copies.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: Use distances 5 for primary and 50 for backup. The same preference and failure checks should pass. Reverse them to see the normal-preference feedback.

scenarios.title: Recover an IPv6 branch handover
scenarios.summary: Combine prefix repair, scoped routing, forwarding and return-path diagnosis.
scenarios.objective: Restore Client’s access to R2’s branch address 2001:db8:20::1 and Server at 2001:db8:20::20, including replies. Client must keep address 2001:db8:10::10 with the correct /64. Keep all other supplied address/prefix settings, including link-local-only transit interfaces. Investigate Client, R1 and Server; repair the source prefix, transit forwarding/next hop and server return route. R1 must forward between its networks.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Combine prefix repair, scoped routing, forwarding and return-path diagnosis.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Verify the complete path

guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: The wrong Client prefix first sends remote traffic onto the local link. After correcting /64, R1 must forward to R2 through the transit-scoped neighbor. R2 can deliver to its branch interface and server, but the server still needs a route back through R2. Each repair has a distinct state effect; the final two-destination verification catches partial recovery.

A correct Client /64, enabled R1 forwarding and a reachable R2 transit next hop solve different parts of the path.
If the branch router responds but the server fails, inspect the server’s return route. Forward delivery and a reply are separate results in the inspector.

concepts.text: Use the full task as a checklist: source prefix, selected next hop, transit forwarding and return route. Inspect applied paths after a check; a later failure can become visible only after an earlier fault is repaired.

concepts.title: Verify more than the gateway
concepts.text: Reaching a router’s own branch address does not prove the server has a reply route. Test both required destinations and keep the supplied address values. This capstone combines earlier concepts and native fields; no new command syntax is required.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: The practice branch has a wrong Client prefix, disabled R1 forwarding, a bad R1 transit next hop and no Server return route. Restore Client’s /64, enable R1 forwarding, route the branch through R2 at fe80::2 on transit, and give Server a default through fe80::1 on lan.

outcomes.label: Office reaches branch service and receives reply

scenarios.title: Protect the report heading
scenarios.summary: Debug a helper that overwrites the caller’s report title.
scenarios.objective: Repair the report printer. REPORT_TITLE is supplied by the lab; each script argument is one item. Print Report: TITLE, then Item: VALUE for every argument in order, then End: TITLE, each on its own line. Keep the original title, spaces, percent signs and empty items. With no items still print the opening and ending lines. Return 0, print no errors and change no files. Bash-specific local is available; equivalent supported repairs are accepted.

hints: Run the starter and compare the first and last lines. Which assignment changes the report title?
Function arguments are separate, but named variables are shared unless you declare a function-local variable.
A local declaration inside print_item can protect the caller’s REPORT_TITLE. Use double quotes when printing values.
scenarios.simplifications: Bash-specific local declarations are available with default Bash scope behavior. They are not portable POSIX sh syntax. No arrays, custom IFS, local options or function-call redirection. Redirect individual commands inside a function. initial.source:
print_item() {
    REPORT_TITLE=$1
    printf 'Item: %s\n' "$REPORT_TITLE"
}
printf 'Report: %s\n' "$REPORT_TITLE"
for item in "$@"; do
    print_item "$item"
done
printf 'End: %s\n' "$REPORT_TITLE"

print_item() {
    local REPORT_TITLE="$1"
    printf 'Item: %s\n' "$REPORT_TITLE"
}
printf 'Report: %s\n' "$REPORT_TITLE"
for item in "$@"; do
    print_item "$item"
done
printf 'End: %s\n' "$REPORT_TITLE"

concepts.title: A helper can change its caller’s variables
concepts.text: Function arguments such as $1 belong to that call. Named variables such as title are shared by default: assigning title inside a helper can replace the caller’s title. The practical task is to find and repair that collision.

concepts.title: Give a helper its own temporary value
concepts.text: Inside a function, local title="$1" gives that call a separate title value. When the function returns, the earlier value becomes visible again. local belongs to Bash; portable sh scripts can pass arguments directly or use carefully chosen names instead.

concepts.title: Read the example, then experiment
concepts.text: The example creates its own title; the lab does not supply it. Inside prints the item, while Outside still prints Weekend notes. In the assignment, REPORT_TITLE is supplied by the lab and item is created by the script. The same protection is useful even when the item is empty.

teaching.example:
title='Weekend notes'
show_item() {
    local title="$1"
    printf 'Inside: %s\n' "$title"
}
show_item 'Spare cable'
printf 'Outside: %s\n' "$title"
teaching.inputs: No arguments, files or supplied variables. The example creates title itself.
teaching.try_change: Remove local before title in show_item and run again. Compare the Outside line; restore local when finished.

concepts.title: Follow the active call
concepts.text: A function-local variable is also visible to helpers it calls. In this example visit gives tone a temporary value, and announce sees that value. After visit returns, the outer tone is visible again. This Bash behavior is called dynamic scope.

concepts.title: Local does not make a variable untouchable
concepts.text: A called helper that assigns tone without its own local declaration can change the caller’s local tone. Prefer explicit arguments for a reusable helper, or clearly document which caller setting it reads. Both styles can solve the assignment.

concepts.title: No matching line is a normal result
concepts.text: grep -F selects lines containing the literal text. It returns 1 when nothing matched. The assignment still prints a topic heading and finishes the full review; a final successful printf can make the overall script return 0. The log always exists in this activity.

teaching.inputs: No files, arguments or supplied variables. The example creates tone.
teaching.try_change: Change loud to busy inside visit and run again. Only the first Tone line should change.

scenarios.retry_guidance: If matching lines are wrong, trace the topic used by grep. If the final Review text names the second topic, the helper leaked its setting into the caller. A quiet topic should not prevent the final summary.
scenarios.explanation: Bash function-local values are visible to functions called from that function. review can temporarily bind needle for matches, then restore the outer value. This is dynamic visibility, not a private variable that no other function can see. Explicitly passing a topic to the filtering helper is often clearer and passes the same tests. A no-match grep is a normal empty selection, not a missing-file failure.

scenarios.title: Repair a review that damages its inputs
scenarios.summary: Protect caller settings and original files in a multi-source review builder.
scenarios.objective: Repair the review builder before trusting it with inputs. Arguments are an output filename, a nonempty literal selection text, then one or more source filenames. Supplied filenames are single names without directory parts and never start with a hyphen; the selection text stays on one line and never starts with a hyphen. First verify every source exists and none is the output. On failure print only Cannot build review plus a newline to standard error, return 2, and leave all files unchanged (do not create output). On success replace the output with Review: TEXT, then for each source in argument order append File: NAME and its matching lines. Keep headings even for no matches; repeated sources are included again. Finish by printing Saved: OUTPUT plus a newline; return 0 with no errors. Preserve all source files. Bash-specific local or equivalent supported repairs are accepted.

hints: Run the starter and inspect files, not just printed text. The checking helper reuses the destination name.
Checking a source must not change the caller’s output filename. A local destination inside valid_source protects it during each call.
Finish every validation before the first >. Then replace the output once and append each section; grep returning 1 for no match is not a failed preflight.

Supplied selection strings are single-line, nonempty and do not begin with a hyphen; supplied filenames are canonical single names without slash components or dot/dot-dot aliases.

initial.source:
valid_source() {
    destination=$1
    if [ "$destination" = "$2" ]; then return 1; fi
    if [ -f "$destination" ]; then return 0; fi
    return 1
}
if [ "$#" -lt 3 ] || [ -z "$2" ]; then
    printf 'Cannot build review\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
destination=$1
needle=$2
shift 2
for path in "$@"; do
    if valid_source "$path" "$destination"; then
        :
    else
        printf 'Cannot build review\n' >&2
        exit 2
    fi
done
printf 'Review: %s\n' "$needle" > "$destination"
for path in "$@"; do
    printf 'File: %s\n' "$path" >> "$destination"
    grep -F "$needle" "$path" >> "$destination"
done
printf 'Saved: %s\n' "$destination"

after./work/review.txt:
Review: ERROR
File: api.log
ERROR timeout
File: db.log
ERROR disk

after./work/out.txt:

File: quiet.log

File: active.log

}
if [ "$#" -lt 3 ] || [ -z "$2" ]; then
    printf 'Cannot build review\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
destination=$1
needle=$2
shift 2
for path in "$@"; do
    if valid_source "$path" "$destination"; then

        exit 2
    fi
done
printf 'Review: %s\n' "$needle" > "$destination"
for path in "$@"; do

concepts.title: Protect settings during preflight
concepts.text: The example checks menu.txt while keeping the caller’s summary.txt destination. Remove local and the helper silently replaces that destination. In the assignment, finish checking every source and reject output/input aliases before opening any file for writing. Supplied names have no directory parts, so this exercise compares names as text. Real files can have different paths to the same file; a text comparison alone is not general alias protection.

concepts.title: Build the report in two phases
concepts.text: After validation, use > once for the report heading, then >> for each source heading and matching lines. Redirect commands inside functions, if used; this simulator does not support redirecting a whole function call. A quiet source still needs its heading.

    if [ -f "$destination" ]; then return 0; fi

teaching.try_change: Remove local before destination inside exists and run again. Watch the destination printed by the caller; no simulated file is changed by this example.

scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare source files as well as the destination. A changed input suggests the validation helper overwrote a caller setting. scenarios.explanation: The preflight helper’s scratch destination name originally replaced the caller’s output setting. Later writes could then target a source file. Giving the helper its own binding—or using separate names/arguments—keeps the output stable. Complete existence and output-alias checks before any redirection. The model uses flat virtual text files and does not claim real filesystem transactions. Output/input comparison here is limited to the supplied canonical single filenames; it does not model real filesystem aliases or links.

concepts.title: Make the order predictable

concepts.title: Keep one copy of each identical line
concepts.text: sort -u combines sorting with removing identical lines, even when the original copies were far apart. It does not merge desk A with desk  A, because their spacing differs. The original file is left unchanged.

concepts.title: Print output or save it deliberately
concepts.text: The example prints its result. A > redirection would replace a destination file, as in the earlier report lessons. The assignment only needs printed output; do not edit or overwrite its input.

scenarios.explanation: Sorting complete lines keeps the list in a repeatable order without changing its names. -u removes identical sorted lines. An equivalent sort followed by adjacent deduplication also works; unsorted adjacent deduplication alone can miss separated copies.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Use cut, whole-line sorting and pipelines from the previous two activities. This lesson introduces adjacent groups and uniq counts.

concepts.title: Adjacent means next to each other
concepts.text: uniq combines runs of identical neighboring lines. It does not remember a name that appeared much earlier. sort first when you want all copies of a location to become one neighboring group.

concepts.title: Count a group without removing its evidence
concepts.text: uniq -c prints how many input lines were in each group. The GNU-style count uses a seven-character-wide space-padded column followed by a space and the original value. Let the utility format it; no manual padding is needed. sort -u first would throw away the counts you need.

concepts.title: Transform records in useful stages
concepts.text: The assignment starts with location:asset records. cut selects locations, sort puts equal values together, and uniq -c counts them. The example already contains one item per line, so it needs only the final two stages.

teaching.example: sort queue.txt | uniq -c
teaching.inputs: queue.txt contains plug, cable, plug, cable, cable, on separate lines. No arguments or supplied variables.
teaching.try_change: Change -c to -d and run again. Repeated items are listed once, without counts.

scenarios.retry_guidance: Counts split into several entries for the same location mean identical lines were not made adjacent. Counts of 1 everywhere may mean -u removed duplicates before counting. Compare spaces and the empty-location group carefully.
scenarios.explanation: Extract fields before grouping so different asset names do not keep the same location apart. Sorting makes equal location lines adjacent. uniq -c counts every record in that group and provides consistent spacing; empty selected fields remain real empty lines.

solution:
if [ "$#" -ne 2 ] || [ -z "$2" ] || [ "$1" = "$2" ]; then
    printf 'Cannot audit inventory\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi

teaching.prerequisite_note: Combines the three text-processing lessons with validation, exit status and safe redirection from the earlier report capstone. This lesson introduces uniq -d as the repeated-groups filter.

concepts.title: An identity collision can hide in different rows
concepts.text: If cable appears in both cable:Store and cable:Desk, the full lines differ but the ID is duplicated. Select the identity field before deciding what repeats. Note lines without a colon are not records in this deliberately simple format.

concepts.title: Select repeated groups
concepts.text: After sort makes equal IDs neighbors, uniq -d prints each group with two or more members once. uniq alone also prints singletons; sort -u removes the evidence of repetition. The small example finds repeated IDs without writing a report.

concepts.title: Protect data before publishing a report
concepts.text: Validate both arguments and the source before any > or >>. Then replace the report heading and append the duplicate list. Supplied names are canonical single filenames; real filesystem links/alternate paths require more than textual equality, outside this activity.

teaching.example: cut -s -d : -f 1 labels.txt | sort | uniq -d
teaching.inputs: labels.txt contains cable:Store, plug:Lab, cable:Desk and note only, on separate lines.
teaching.try_change: Change -d to -u and run again. Now only the ID that occurred once is printed.

scenarios.retry_guidance: If single-use IDs appear, the last stage is not repeated-only selection. If a repeated ID is missing, check that sorting happens before grouping. If invalid input changes files, move redirection after validation.
scenarios.explanation: The pipeline answers a different question at each stage: which ID is in this row, which equal IDs can be grouped, and which groups contain more than one row? A heading-only report is a valid success when no duplicates exist. Validation precedes replacement so a missing source cannot destroy the old audit. The comparison applies only to the supplied simple filenames, not every real alias or file format.

Count blank records too; an empty file prints nothing. Keep internal spaces, backslashes and percent signs literal. A final nonempty record may lack a newline. Return 0, print no errors and leave every file unchanged. Supplied records have no edge spaces or tabs.
scenarios.retry_guidance: If numbering restarts at 1, check where you initialize the counter. If the last row is missing, check EOF handling. Blank rows must still receive a number.

hints: Start with a counter before the loop. Add one for every successful record, including an empty line.
Use $((number + 1)) to calculate the next value. Writing number=number+1 stores text instead.
Keep the EOF-safe condition from the earlier input lesson. Print the number and original record with separate %s values.

Only small supplied nonnegative integers are calculated; no floating-point math, arithmetic commands, recursive variable expressions or general numeric-input validation. Named inputs are canonical single /work filenames without directory parts or leading hyphens. Text records have no leading/trailing spaces or tabs; internal spaces/backslashes/percent signs stay literal. Flat virtual files only; bounded simulation, never host execution.

initial.source:
# Number each record, including blanks and the final record.
number=0
