concepts.title: A total accumulates quantities
concepts.text: A counter adds one for each record. A total adds the quantity in the record: total=$((total + quantity)). Start at zero outside the loop. Replacing the total with the latest quantity loses previous work; joining strings produces text, not addition.

concepts.title: Multiply units by a rate
concepts.text: The * operator multiplies. If one item costs 8 cents, three items cost 3 * 8 = 24 cents. Multiplication happens before addition, so boxes * price + fee adds the fee after multiplying. Parentheses can make a different grouping explicit.

concepts.title: Whole cents avoid rounding here
concepts.text: The assignment supplies small valid whole numbers: quantities 0 to 999, at most 64 records, and a price from 0 to 99 cents. Values have no leading zeros or signs; there are no blank records. You are calculating, not validating arbitrary user text. A zero rate is valid; empty input totals zero. No decimal fractions are supported.

teaching.example:
boxes=3
price=8
fee=2
charge=$((boxes * price + fee))
printf 'Charge (cents): %s\n' "$charge"

teaching.try_change: Change boxes * price + fee to boxes * (price + fee) and run again. The charge becomes 30 because the fee is now included once per box.

scenarios.explanation: Addition accumulates quantities; multiplication applies a rate. Multiplying each row and summing gives the same result as multiplying the final total. Working in whole cents avoids pretending this shell subset performs decimal money arithmetic.

initial.source:
# Validate argument count and nonzero capacity before calculating.
# Build a packing plan from the supplied $1 and $2 values.

solution:
if [ "$#" -ne 2 ]; then
    printf 'Cannot pack items\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
items=$1
capacity=$2
if [ "$capacity" -eq 0 ]; then
    printf 'Cannot pack items\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
cartons=$((items / capacity))
loose=$((items % capacity))
printf 'Full cartons: %s\nLoose items: %s\n' "$cartons" "$loose"

teaching.prerequisite_note: Uses earlier argument-count guards, if/test, separate error output and arithmetic totals. The task supplies valid integer notation; checking arbitrary text is outside this unit.

concepts.title: Whole groups and leftovers answer different questions
concepts.text: Integer / counts only complete groups: 17 / 5 is 3, not 3.4. The % operator gives what is left: 17 % 5 is 2. For nonnegative items and a positive capacity, items = full * capacity + leftover, and leftover is smaller than capacity. A partial carton is not a full carton.

concepts.title: Check before dividing
concepts.text: Zero cannot be a divisor. [ "$tray" -gt 0 ] asks whether tray is greater than zero; -eq means equal and -ne means not equal. These comparisons belong inside [ ], separate from $(( )) calculations. A rejected request should print a useful error and exit before division, not crash during calculation.

concepts.title: Count supplied arguments before using them
concepts.text: The earlier "$#" value is the number of supplied arguments. Reject missing or extra values before reading them as numbers. All provided numeric values here are small nonnegative decimal integers without leading zeros. This guard is not a validator for arbitrary shell arithmetic text.

teaching.example:
items=17
tray=5
if [ "$tray" -gt 0 ]; then
    full=$((items / tray))
    left=$((items % tray))
    printf 'Trays: %s; spare: %s\n' "$full" "$left"
else
    printf 'Choose a nonzero tray size\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
teaching.inputs: The example creates items=17 and tray=5, then prints three trays and two spare items. No files or assignment inputs are used.
teaching.try_change: Change tray=5 to tray=0 and run again. The guard prints the nonzero-size message on the error channel and exits 2 without dividing.

scenarios.explanation: For positive capacities, integer division discards the fractional part, leaving only full cartons. The remainder accounts for everything else. Argument and zero-capacity guards make invalid requests predictable without attempting impossible arithmetic.

cases.name: Destination is also a later input

solution:
if [ "$#" -lt 2 ] || [ -z "$1" ]; then
    printf 'Cannot count files\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
destination=$1
shift
for file in "$@"; do
    if [ "$file" = "$destination" ]; then
        printf 'Cannot count files\n' >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    if [ -f "$file" ]; then
        :
    else
        printf 'Cannot count files\n' >&2
        exit 2
    fi
done
total=0
printf 'Record counts\n' > "$destination"
for file in "$@"; do
    count=0
    while read -r row || [ -n "$row" ]; do
        count=$((count + 1))
    done < "$file"
    printf '%s: %s\n' "$file" "$count" >> "$destination"
    total=$((total + count))
done
printf 'Total: %s\n' "$total" >> "$destination"
printf 'Saved: %s\n' "$destination"

teaching.prerequisite_note: Combines record counting with "$@", shift, file checks and validate-before-writing from the reusable bundle capstone. No new syntax is required. A helper function is optional.

concepts.title: Reset each file count, keep the grand total
concepts.text: Initialize total before the outer loop. Initialize count inside that loop, before reading each file. Otherwise the second file inherits the first file's count. Add each finished count to the total once. If a name occurs twice, the request asks for two counts, in the same order.

concepts.title: Preflight the whole request before publishing
concepts.text: The first pass checks every source and protects the destination from also being a source. Only a fully valid request may create or replace the report. A second pass performs counting. Checking each file just before reading it is too late if an earlier write has already destroyed the old report.

concepts.text: These supplied filenames are simple canonical names with no directory parts. Comparing their text is sufficient for this exercise, not a guarantee about links or alternate paths in a real filesystem. All reading/writing here occurs in the simulator. Finite records and files keep this exercise within execution limits.

teaching.example:

for file in morning.txt evening.txt; do
    count=0
    while read -r note || [ -n "$note" ]; do
        count=$((count + 1))
    done < "$file"
    printf '%s: %s\n' "$file" "$count"
    total=$((total + count))
done
printf 'Combined: %s\n' "$total"
teaching.inputs: morning.txt contains two notes and evening.txt one note. The example prints each file count and a combined total; it does not publish a report.
teaching.try_change: Change total + count to total + 1 and run again. Combined becomes 2, counting files instead of records. The individual file counts stay unchanged.

scenarios.explanation: Two passes separate validation from mutation. The per-file counter starts again for each request entry, while the total spans all entries. This makes repeated sources explicit rather than accidentally deduplicated. EOF-safe reads retain final records and valid blank records without inventing an extra record for an empty file.

terminal_teaching.prerequisite_note: Uses copy-versus-move and group access. You now distinguish writing an existing file from creating/replacing a directory entry.

concepts.title: Writing data is different from changing a name
concepts.text: An existing file with write permission can be updated without directory write permission. The parent still needs search. Creating a new file, removing one or renaming one requires parent write/search. A directory can therefore prevent new names while allowing selected existing files to change.

concepts.title: Use the permission class that actually applies
concepts.text: The example label belongs to Blair, group staff. Alex is not its owner but belongs to staff and has group write. Alex cannot chmod Blair's file. Ordinary cp to an existing writable file updates its content while retaining its owner/group/mode; removing and recreating it would give the replacement a new owner.

concepts.title: Preserve evidence while choosing the correct source
concepts.text: Inspect the incoming text with cat, then copy rather than move it. Check the result and directory permissions. The assignment includes an obsolete roster as a deliberate investigation choice; successful execution alone does not prove you selected the right input.

terminal_teaching.inputs: The cabinet is 550 and Alex belongs to its group. The example updates an existing group-writable label owned by Blair, without adding directory write permission.
terminal_teaching.try_change: Try touch cabinet/new.txt. It must fail without creating a file: updating a writable existing file did not grant permission to create a new name.

scenarios.explanation: Directory read-only does not make every contained file read-only. Parent search reaches the existing entry; group write permits its data to change. Copying into that existing file retains the other owner, whereas deleting and creating a replacement would not.

scenarios.title: Retire a read-only handover safely
scenarios.summary: Preserve file identity while restoring a locked-down staging policy.
scenarios.objective: Rename /work/staging/ready.txt to delivered.txt, preserving its approved receipt text, owner blair, group review and mode 444. ready.txt must be gone afterward. Keep proof.txt with its original text and mode 600. Finish with staging owned by alex/group staff at mode 500. Work as alex without root. Investigate why the first move is blocked, make only the temporary permission change needed, and restore the final directory policy before Check work.
scenarios.retry_guidance: If mv is blocked, inspect parent write/search rather than adding file write. If ownership changed, inspect whether you copied and recreated it. If the folder is still writable, finish the temporary-permission cleanup.

guide.title: Inspect the current permissions
guide.why: The same permission letter has a different effect on a file and its parent directory.
guide.action: Use ls -l for files, ls -ld for directories and id for the supplied memberships. You work as alex; root is not available.

commands.explanation: Inspect the directory itself rather than listing its contents.

guide.title: Make the smallest safe change
guide.why: A targeted change avoids opening access for unrelated people or damaging another owner's files.
guide.action: Repair the stated policy and preserve the required evidence. Each command acts only on the simulated tree.

guide.title: Verify the complete outcome
guide.why: A successful command does not prove the whole access requirement is satisfied.
guide.action: Inspect again, then Check work. If something fails, use the current feedback to investigate and retry.

hints: Inspect the directory itself as well as the file. File write permission is not the gate for this rename.
As the directory owner, Alex can temporarily add directory write, then move the existing entry. Keep its identity rather than recreating it.
Restore the final 500 directory mode after the move. A renamed file alone is only partial completion.
scenarios.simplifications: Ordinary simulated user alex, canonical virtual tree and traditional owner/group/other permissions only. No root/sudo, account changes, ACL/SELinux, links, special bits, mounts or actual execution of files. chmod supports numeric modes or explicit u/g/o/a r/w/x clauses; chgrp requires ownership and membership. id uses supplied identities with synthetic numbers. Group membership is fixed; no real accounts or files are touched. Only supported literal commands; no shell expansion/redirection/pipelines. See optional command reference.

terminal_teaching.prerequisite_note: Combines file-versus-directory permissions, safe moves and preservation checks. No new command syntax is required; this is an independent repair/handover capstone.

concepts.title: A read-only file can still be renamed
concepts.text: The name is an entry in its parent directory. Renaming or removing it uses the parent's write/search permissions, not the file's write bit. That is why making a file read-only does not protect it from someone who can change its directory.

concepts.title: Keep the other owner's identity
concepts.text: mv within this modeled filesystem preserves the existing file metadata. A new copy belongs to the copying user, so copy-then-remove would lose Blair's ownership here. Alex cannot restore another owner with chmod or chgrp; ownership transfer/root is outside this ordinary-user activity.

concepts.title: Return temporary permission changes to the final policy
concepts.text: The folder owner can temporarily add their own write permission, perform the move, then remove it. Verify the retained proof and final permissions, not merely the existence of the new name. There are no shell scripts or real filesystem actions involved.

terminal_teaching.inputs: Example dispatch starts at 500; its read-only parcel belongs to Blair. After moving it to sent.txt, the folder is 500 again.
terminal_teaching.try_change: Try mv dispatch/sent.txt dispatch/again.txt after the example. It must fail and retain sent.txt because directory write permission has been removed.

scenarios.explanation: The parent controls changes to names; the file mode controls access to its content. A temporary owner-write change permits the rename without editing the read-only file or taking it from its owner. Restoring the parent policy completes the handover.

scenarios.title: Reconnect a workstation to its workgroup
scenarios.summary: Repair group membership on one switch while keeping visitors separate.
scenarios.objective: Two staff workstations must share VLAN 10; two guest workstations must share VLAN 20. Each pair must receive each other’s broadcasts, and staff and guests must stay separate. One port has the wrong group. Inspect the office switch, repair it, then Check configuration. Keep every workstation connected and its port up.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare both workstations and the ports along their path. Keep a working group working while you repair another. Use Inspect broadcast delivery to see where the applied settings send data.
steps: Inspect the stated policy, edit the relevant ports and check the complete configuration.
scenarios.explanation: Both staff ports need access VLAN 10 and both guest ports need access VLAN 20. Broadcasts stay within the local VLAN. Moving staff-b from 20 to 10 restores staff service without merging the groups. Both positive service checks and negative separation checks are necessary; stopping a port proves neither policy nor a usable network.
hints: Match each port’s connected workstation to the two groups in the task.
Compare staff-a and staff-b. The workstation stays connected; its access VLAN determines its group.
scenarios.simplifications: Only bounded broadcast data-plane visibility is simulated, not ping, ARP, MAC learning, STP/PVST, routing, voice VLANs or Cisco commands. Workstations are untagged and fixed to their cables. Trunk native egress is untagged; allowed tagged native ingress follows the documented educational profile, not universal platform behavior. Lists use individual comma-separated VLAN IDs, not IOS range syntax. This is partial CCNA practice, not equipment or full-objective coverage.

switching_teaching.prerequisite_note: Start here: no binary, subnetting or command-line knowledge is needed. Select Assignment whenever you are ready; your example and assignment are saved separately.

concepts.title: One cable, several groups
concepts.text: A switch connects workstations through named ports. A broadcast is a message offered to every other workstation in its group. A virtual local area network (VLAN) makes separate broadcast groups on the same switch; it is not an IP address or subnet mask.

concepts.title: Choose the workstation’s group
concepts.text: An access port puts an ordinary workstation’s untagged messages into one VLAN. Up means the port can carry data. Keep the mode Access and edit its VLAN number. The number names a group, not the workstation. The group must also appear in Active VLANs.

concepts.title: Inspect, edit, check
concepts.text: The port row says which workstation is connected. Changes are saved as a draft; Check configuration applies and tests them together. Pass results use both directions and do not count unplugging a workstation as separation. Optional broadcast inspection shows applied settings, not unsaved edits.

switching_teaching.example_description: A separate office uses studio VLAN 30 and visitor VLAN 40. Studio B is in the wrong group. Inspect its row, change the access VLAN to 30, and Apply and test example. Load example settings can fill the repair on request.
switching_teaching.try_change: Change studio-b back to VLAN 40 and apply. Studio service fails even though the visitor pair can still work; restore 30.

scenarios.title: Carry two groups between offices
scenarios.summary: Build a trunk and repair the difference between an active group and an allowed group.
scenarios.objective: Staff VLAN 10 and guest VLAN 20 each span west and east switches. Restore two-way broadcast delivery within each group and separation between groups. Keep workstation access memberships. The inter-switch uplinks must be up trunks using native VLAN 99. Investigate uplink modes, active VLANs and allowed lists; repair every fault, then check.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare both workstations and the ports along their path. Keep a working group working while you repair another. Use Inspect broadcast delivery to see where the applied settings send data.
steps: Inspect the stated policy, edit the relevant ports and check the complete configuration.
scenarios.explanation: A trunk needs compatible mode and native settings at both ends. Staff and guest VLANs must exist in both switches and be allowed along the link. Correcting the west mode alone leaves guest service broken because the east database and allowed list also omit 20. Extra unused allowed VLANs do not replace the required groups; the grader checks current service and separation, not one exact list string.
hints: First check that both uplinks use Trunk. An access port can classify only one untagged group.
A guest frame needs VLAN 20 active on each switch and allowed at both trunk ends. These are different settings.
scenarios.simplifications: Only bounded broadcast data-plane visibility is simulated, not ping, ARP, MAC learning, STP/PVST, routing, voice VLANs or Cisco commands. Workstations are untagged and fixed to their cables. Trunk native egress is untagged; allowed tagged native ingress follows the documented educational profile, not universal platform behavior. Lists use individual comma-separated VLAN IDs, not IOS range syntax. This is partial CCNA practice, not equipment or full-objective coverage.

switching_teaching.prerequisite_note: First try Reconnect a workstation to its workgroup. You should recognize access ports, VLAN group numbers, drafts and the difference between service and separation.

concepts.title: Carry several groups over one cable
concepts.text: An inter-switch trunk can carry several VLANs. A tag is a small label added to a frame on that cable, so the next switch knows its group. Workstation access links remain untagged. A trunk at only one end is not a complete repair.

concepts.title: Two separate permissions to travel
concepts.text: Active VLANs lists groups that exist on this switch. A trunk’s Allowed VLANs lists the groups permitted over that port. A number in an access field or allowed list does not create an active VLAN. Check both switches and both trunk ends.

concepts.title: The native group is the untagged exception
concepts.text: This model sends the trunk’s native VLAN without a tag; other allowed VLANs carry tags. Both ends must agree. Use the task’s native VLAN 99 here, which has no workstation. Enter lists as 10,20,99; ranges such as 10-20 are outside these editors.

switching_teaching.example_description: The example connects studio VLAN 30 and visitor VLAN 40 across two switches, with native VLAN 90. The west uplink is still Access; east is missing the visitor group from both its active database and allowed list. Repair those three settings, then apply.
switching_teaching.try_change: After the repair, remove 40 only from the east uplink’s allowed list and apply. The group still exists, but visitor traffic cannot cross. Restore 40.

scenarios.title: Align the meaning of untagged traffic
scenarios.summary: Trace native-VLAN classification in a restricted data-plane exercise.
scenarios.objective: In this data-plane exercise, west uses native VLAN 10 and east uses native VLAN 20. Staff VLAN 10 and guests VLAN 20 must each work across the link and stay separate. Adopt the requested native VLAN 99 at both up trunk ends, keep the stated access memberships, and verify both delivery directions. Actual Catalyst PVST can block native mismatches; that protection is not simulated here.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare both workstations and the ports along their path. Keep a working group working while you repair another. Use Inspect broadcast delivery to see where the applied settings send data.
steps: Inspect the stated policy, edit the relevant ports and check the complete configuration.
scenarios.explanation: With the requested native VLAN 99 at both ends, staff 10 and guest 20 travel tagged and the far switch retains their groups. Initially, untagged native traffic can be reclassified into the other group in this restricted model. Aligning just one end is incomplete. Real PVST/PVID protection may instead block mismatches; this lesson does not model or certify that control behavior.
hints: An untagged frame has no group number on the cable. Each receiving trunk supplies its own native VLAN.
Use native VLAN 99 at both uplinks, as requested. Keep 10 and 20 in their active/allowed groups.
scenarios.simplifications: Only bounded broadcast data-plane visibility is simulated, not ping, ARP, MAC learning, STP/PVST, routing, voice VLANs or Cisco commands. Workstations are untagged and fixed to their cables. Trunk native egress is untagged; allowed tagged native ingress follows the documented educational profile, not universal platform behavior. Lists use individual comma-separated VLAN IDs, not IOS range syntax. This is partial CCNA practice, not equipment or full-objective coverage.

switching_teaching.prerequisite_note: Complete Carry two groups between offices first. This exercise examines data classification, not a prediction that every real switch will forward a native mismatch.

concepts.title: Untagged does not mean no group
concepts.text: An untagged frame arriving on a trunk enters that receiving port’s native VLAN. A tagged frame uses its allowed tag in this educational profile. Egress in the native group loses its tag. The receiver cannot recover the sender’s group number from an absent tag.

concepts.title: A disagreement can change the group
concepts.text: If one end sends its VLAN 30 untagged and the far end treats untagged data as VLAN 40, this restricted data plane places it in group 40. Check both directions: a one-way path is not full service, and a one-way leak is not separation.

concepts.title: Real control protocols add protection
concepts.text: Real Catalyst PVST/PVID inconsistency detection can block a mismatched port, even on a simple tree. It is excluded here, along with STP and MAC learning. Use this lesson to understand tagging/classification; do not infer actual equipment forwarding or a troubleshooting command sequence.

switching_teaching.example_description: The studio/visitor example has native VLAN 30 at west and 40 at east. Inspect the applied broadcast recipients. Set both trunk native fields to the example’s reserved VLAN 90, keep both groups allowed, and apply.
switching_teaching.try_change: After repair, change only the east native field to 40 and apply. Inspect visitor-west and visitor-east in turn: one direction can still work while the reverse fails. Restore native 90.

scenarios.title: Hand over three working, separate groups
scenarios.summary: Diagnose several interacting faults and verify the whole office policy.
scenarios.objective: Hand over a two-switch office with three groups: staff VLAN 10, guests VLAN 20 and operations VLAN 30. Each west/east pair must exchange broadcasts in both directions; every group must remain separate from the others. Configure all six access ports with the stated memberships and use native VLAN 99 on both up trunks. Inspect all settings and applied delivery evidence, repair the interacting faults, and Check configuration. Keep every workstation connected and working.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare both workstations and the ports along their path. Keep a working group working while you repair another. Use Inspect broadcast delivery to see where the applied settings send data.
steps: Inspect the stated policy, edit the relevant ports and check the complete configuration.
scenarios.explanation: The handover requires five different repairs: operations-west joins access VLAN 30; east activates guest VLAN 20; west allows operations 30 across its trunk; east changes native to 99; and the east guest access port comes up. Correct access/native policy plus all positive and negative delivery cases rules out a partial repair or shutdown shortcut. Equivalent allowed-list order and extra unused active/allowed groups are accepted when the stated service and separation remain correct.
hints: Check every host port’s access group and Up state before following the uplinks. A stopped guest is not successful isolation.
Operations needs 30 on both active databases and allowed trunk lists. The guest VLAN must exist on east even after its port is brought up.
Both trunks must use native 99. Repairing just access membership, just trunk permissions, or just link state is partial work.
scenarios.simplifications: Only bounded broadcast data-plane visibility is simulated, not ping, ARP, MAC learning, STP/PVST, routing, voice VLANs or Cisco commands. Workstations are untagged and fixed to their cables. Trunk native egress is untagged; allowed tagged native ingress follows the documented educational profile, not universal platform behavior. Lists use individual comma-separated VLAN IDs, not IOS range syntax. This is partial CCNA practice, not equipment or full-objective coverage.

switching_teaching.prerequisite_note: This capstone combines the preceding three lessons: access membership, active VLAN databases, allowed trunk lists, native classification and checking both directions.

concepts.title: Keep the full policy in view
concepts.text: A single passing path does not prove the office works. Each group needs its own west/east service, plus separation from the other groups. A down port can hide a wrong configuration, so all six workstations must remain operational.

concepts.title: Investigate in layers
concepts.text: Start with the named workstation’s access mode, VLAN and Up state. Follow the cable to both trunks, then check the active database and allowed list on each switch. Use the applied broadcast inspector to test a hypothesis. Change one cause at a time if it helps; the complete assignment remains visible.

concepts.title: Verify the handover, not only the repair
concepts.text: Recheck working groups after every change. Check configuration evaluates the whole current policy and clears stale success after edits. The example is a different practice office; loading or completing it cannot earn the assignment.

switching_teaching.example_description: The practice handover has design 50, visitors 60 and support 70, with native 90. Support-west has the wrong access group; visitors-east is stopped and its VLAN is absent on east; west omits support from the trunk; east has the wrong native group. Repair all five causes and apply.
switching_teaching.try_change: After a complete example, remove only VLAN 70 from the east active list and apply. Design and visitors can work while support fails. Restore 70 and recheck.

scenarios.title: Build a changing file manifest
scenarios.summary: Select visible logs by name while preserving spaces and empty inputs.
scenarios.objective: Replace manifest.txt with one filename per line for every visible file ending in .log, in C-locale filename order. Keep filenames literal, including spaces, backslashes, percent signs and UTF-8. Exclude hidden files and other endings. With no matches create an empty manifest. Print nothing, return 0 and preserve every other file. The lab supplies the files; your script discovers the current selection rather than listing fixed names.
scenarios.retry_guidance: If a name breaks at spaces, inspect quotes around the loop variable. If only the last name survives, check where > is used. A literal *.log line means the no-match case needs attention.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Each test starts with its own sample inputs. Simulated files reset before each test; your editor draft stays saved.
guide.action: Replace manifest.txt with one filename per line for every visible file ending in .log, in C-locale filename order. Keep filenames literal, including spaces, backslashes, percent signs and UTF-8. Exclude hidden files and other endings. With no matches create an empty manifest. Print nothing, return 0 and preserve every other file. The lab supplies the files; your script discovers the current selection rather than listing fixed names.

guide.why: The same script must handle a changed set of files, not just the first example.
guide.action: Open input details when useful. Compare expected and actual output and files after Run.

guide.title: Build, run and investigate
guide.why: Select sources deliberately and keep data separate from shell instructions.
guide.action: Run, inspect the first differing input set, edit and retry. Help is optional.

hints: Leave the intended *.log pattern unquoted in the for list; quote the selected filename everywhere it is used.
Initialize manifest.txt once. Replacing it inside the loop retains only the last entry.
Guard each selected value with a file test so no-match text does not become a fake filename.

Unquoted * and ? only: no bracket, recursive or directory patterns. Hidden files require an explicit leading dot. Names in these assignments have no newline or leading hyphen. Fixed virtual input files always remain unchanged; bounded simulation. Text matching is case-sensitive literal substring matching, not regular expressions. This is authored practice, not full shell or certification coverage.

initial.source:
# Discover the visible .log files; do not hardcode their names.
# Replace manifest.txt once, then add each whole filename.

cases.name: Empty file still has a name

solution:
printf '' > manifest.txt
for file in *.log; do
    if [ -f "$file" ]; then
        printf '%s\n' "$file" >> manifest.txt
    fi
done

teaching.example:
printf '' > list.txt
for item in *.note; do
    if [ -f "$item" ]; then
        printf '%s\n' "$item" >> list.txt
    fi
done
teaching.inputs: The example supplies two visible .note files, a hidden note and an old list.txt. The script creates item; no variable is supplied by the lab. Inspect the resulting list in virtual files.
teaching.try_change: Change *.note to *.missing and Run. There are no matches: list.txt becomes empty, and the literal pattern is not listed because the file test fails.

concepts.title: Let the shell discover names
concepts.text: A filename pattern selects a changing set of files. In *.note, * means any number of filename bytes and .note is literal. The shell replaces this unquoted pattern with matching names before the command or for loop begins. A loop gets one whole filename per item, even if a matching name contains spaces.

concepts.title: Quote the selected name
concepts.text: After selection, "$item" passes the current filename as one argument. Writing $item can split a name at spaces and start another filename search. Quote values; leave only the pattern that you intend to expand unquoted.

concepts.title: Handle an empty selection
concepts.text: By default, a pattern with no matches stays as literal text. Before processing it, [ -f "$item" ] checks whether it names a file. A leading dot is not selected by *.note. The simulator sorts names in C-byte order, with uppercase before lowercase and UTF-8 names after ASCII.

concepts.title: Replace once, append inside
concepts.text: printf with an empty format prints nothing. printf '' > list.txt creates or empties the list once, before the loop. >> inside the loop adds each filename without erasing earlier entries. The output file has a different ending from the sources.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Uses the for loop, if file test, quoted printf values and redirection from scripting foundations. Reopen those lessons if these are unfamiliar; filename matching is introduced here.

scenarios.explanation: Filename matching chooses the real input set before the loop; quoting then preserves each chosen name. A file test distinguishes no-match pattern text from an actual file. Replacing the output once and appending each result preserves the full manifest.

scenarios.title: Collect incidents across a changing log set
scenarios.summary: Combine literal ERROR records without losing duplicates or treating no matches as a broken batch.
scenarios.objective: Replace errors.txt with every line containing the literal text ERROR from visible .log files. Process source filenames in C-locale order and preserve line order and duplicate lines within each source. Include no filenames or headings. A final matching line without a newline gains one in the report. With no files or matches, the report is empty. Return 0, print nothing to either output channel and preserve all input files. Matching is case-sensitive substring matching: NOTERROR contains ERROR too.
scenarios.retry_guidance: If the report repeats filenames, remove unintended labels. If duplicates disappear, sorting or deduplication changed the task. If only the final source remains, check > versus >>. A status 1 with correct empty output may be the last filter result.

A no-match grep status is expected here. Make the finished batch return 0 after processing all sources.

initial.source:
# Collect ERROR lines from the current visible logs.
# Leave inputs unchanged and keep duplicate records.

after./work/errors.txt:
ERROR link
ERROR disk
ERROR disk

NOTERROR still contains the text
ERROR 100% path\west

solution:
printf '' > errors.txt
for file in *.log; do
    if [ -f "$file" ]; then
        grep -F ERROR "$file" >> errors.txt
    fi
done
exit 0

teaching.example:
printf '' > flags.txt
for file in *.note; do
    if [ -f "$file" ]; then
        grep -F TODO "$file" >> flags.txt
    fi
done
exit 0
teaching.inputs: The example uses .note sources and TODO text, not the assignment’s .log/ERROR selection. The script creates file; the lab supplies only files. Open the resulting flags.txt.
teaching.try_change: Change TODO to LATER and Run. flags.txt is empty, and the script still finishes with status 0.

after./work/flags.txt:
TODO visit
TODO pack
TODO pack

concepts.title: Select files, then select records
concepts.text: The filename pattern chooses source files. grep -F TODO "$file" then chooses lines inside one source that contain the exact text TODO. These are two different selections. -F means fixed text, not a regular expression. Matching lines keep their order and duplicates.

concepts.title: No matching line is normal
concepts.text: grep returns 0 when it finds a line and 1 when it does not. A batch can still succeed when some or all files have no matching records. Finish the completed batch with exit 0; do not mistake a normal empty result for a missing command.

concepts.title: Send records into one report
concepts.text: Create or empty the report before the loop. Append each filter result with >>. The example prints no console output because matches go into flags.txt. A final matching record receives a newline; an empty source contributes nothing.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Uses Build a changing file manifest and the literal filter/pipeline lesson. Reopen those prerequisites if grep, redirection or exit status is unfamiliar.

scenarios.explanation: The outer selection chooses visible source files; the inner fixed-text filter chooses records. Appending preserves duplicates and order, while explicit final success describes the completed batch rather than the last file’s match status.

scenarios.title: Publish a safe incident handover
scenarios.summary: Capture the source set before creating a report, reject collisions, and combine selection, filtering and counts.
scenarios.objective:
Publish an incident handover from the visible .log files. Accept exactly one nonempty destination filename. Capture sources before creating or changing it. If the destination is already a selected source, or the argument count/value is invalid, print only Cannot publish audit plus a newline to standard error, return 2, and change no files.

On success, replace the destination with Error audit plus a newline. For each selected source in C-locale order, add File: NAME and its ERROR lines, keeping duplicates and adding a newline to a final matching line. End with Files: COUNT and a newline, counting empty sources too.

Return 0 and print nothing to either console channel. Preserve all inputs and unrelated files. A new .log destination must not become its own source. Supplied destinations are canonical relative filenames without wildcard characters or leading hyphens.
scenarios.retry_guidance: If a new .log report appears in its own contents, selection happened after creation. If a collision damages a source, move all validation before the first write. Count files, not matching records; empty sources still get headings.

solution:
if [ "$#" -ne 1 ] || [ -z "$1" ]; then
    printf 'Cannot publish audit\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
destination=$1
publish() {
    for file in "$@"; do
        if [ -f "$file" ] && [ "$file" = "$destination" ]; then
            printf 'Cannot publish audit\n' >&2
            return 2
        fi
    done
    printf 'Error audit\n' > "$destination"
    count=0
    for file in "$@"; do
        if [ -f "$file" ]; then
            printf 'File: %s\n' "$file" >> "$destination"
            grep -F ERROR "$file" >> "$destination"
            count=$((count + 1))
        fi
    done
    printf 'Files: %s\n' "$count" >> "$destination"
}
publish *.log

build_list() {

        if [ -f "$item" ] && [ "$item" = "$target" ]; then

    done
    printf 'Notes\n' > "$target"
    for item in "$@"; do

concepts.text: Creating a new report ending in .note changes what a later *.note would match. Expanding the pattern at the function call captures the original selection. concepts.text: A matching source might also be the requested destination. Check the entire captured set before > touches anything. Reject a collision rather than replacing input with output. The earlier function/validation lessons supply return, argument counts and if tests.

concepts.title: Give a name an address
concepts.text: DNS lets a readable name stand for data such as a computer address. A zone is the part of DNS you manage. A records hold IPv4 addresses; AAAA records hold IPv6 addresses. All addresses for this exercise are supplied; you do not need to calculate subnets. NS identifies the nameserver responsible for this zone. concepts.title: Write one complete record per line

Type in Resource records. For example: files.dual-practice.test. 300 IN A 192.0.2.140. The name ends with a dot so it is complete. 300 is the TTL in seconds, how long a resolver may cache the answer; caching is not simulated here. IN means Internet class. An IPv6 example is a separate line:
files.dual-practice.test. 300 IN AAAA 2001:db8::140
Keep both A and AAAA records at the same name.

concepts.title: Saved is different from served

concepts.title: Two servers can hold different copies
concepts.text: A primary publishes the saved zone. A secondary keeps another copy for availability. Select Primary or Secondary before an A lookup to compare their answers. A matching name does not prove both have the same revision.

concepts.title: A revision number controls the update
concepts.text: SOA serial is the zone revision number. A primary can load changed data with an equal serial, but the secondary then sees no newer revision and retains its copy. For ordinary small changes, increase the saved serial, save, reload the primary and update the secondary. Any supported newer value is accepted; no particular decimal format is required.

concepts.title: Verify the new value and the peers
concepts.text: Check web on both copies, and preserve api/ns. This explicit Update secondary control models only the serial decision and copy, not DNS transfer packets or refresh timers. Advanced serial wraparound limits are available in the optional references.

A missing first or second request prints a blank value after the colon and space. Then print Task: VALUE for every request in original order. hints: A quoted "$@" provides separate arguments. queue=("$@") preserves those boundaries in a Bash array.
${#queue[@]} counts elements; ${queue[0]} is the first and ${queue[1]} the second. A missing constant index expands to empty.
Use sole quoted "${queue[@]}" in the loop. Joining with $queue or unquoted expansion loses information.

Ordinary scalar assignment updates element 0 and retains the tail. No indexed writes, computed indices, +=, associative/sparse arrays, unset or declaration attributes. Only declared flat /work text files exist; no host commands or files. Equivalent supported programs are accepted by behavior, even if they do not use arrays.

initial.source: # Capture the supplied requests, summarize them, then print the whole queue.

cases.name: Several requests

Standby: Router check
Task: Printer setup
Task: Router check
Task: Backup review

Task:

Standby: B
Task: A
Task: B
Task: C
Task: D

Task: F

solution:
queue=("$@")
printf 'Queue: %s\nNext: %s\nStandby: %s\n' "${#queue[@]}" "${queue[0]}" "${queue[1]}"
for job in "${queue[@]}"; do
    printf 'Task: %s\n' "$job"
done

concepts.title: A variable can hold a list
concepts.text: An array stores separate values under one name. books=('Field guide' '' '*.txt') stores three values: a title, an empty value and literal text. These are elements, or entries in the list. The first entry has index 0, the second index 1.

concepts.title: Read one entry, count entries, or revisit all
concepts.text: ${books[0]} reads one entry. ${#books[@]} counts entries, including empty ones. Sole quoted "${books[@]}" gives each entry separately to a command or loop. The double quotes preserve spaces and protect wildcard text from filename matching.

concepts.title: Capture supplied values without inventing them
concepts.text: The practice example creates books itself; the lab does not supply it. The assignment supplies script arguments, not a variable named queue. Create your own queue with queue=("$@"). An empty list queue=() differs from queue=(''), which contains one empty value.

teaching.example:
books=('Field guide' '' '*.txt')
printf 'Books: %s\nFirst: <%s>\n' "${#books[@]}" "${books[0]}"
for book in "${books[@]}"; do printf 'Book: <%s>\n' "$book"; done
teaching.inputs: No arguments or supplied variables. The example creates books; a.txt exists only to show that quoted wildcard text stays literal.
teaching.try_change: Add a fourth title, then replace the list with books=() and rerun. Compare the count and the number of Book lines.

cases.stdout:

ready

a

solution:
if [ "$#" -lt 3 ]; then printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
mode=$1
destination=$2
shift 2
sources=("$@")
if [ "$mode" = preview ] || [ "$mode" = save ]; then :; else
    printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2
fi
if [ -z "$destination" ]; then printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
for file in "${sources[@]}"; do
    if [ -z "$file" ] || [ "$file" = "$destination" ]; then
        printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2
    fi
    if [ -f "$file" ]; then :; else printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
done
report() {
    printf 'Handover\nFiles: %s\n' "${#sources[@]}"
    for file in "${sources[@]}"; do
        printf 'Source: %s\n' "$file"
        cat "$file"
    done
}
if [ "$mode" = preview ]; then
    report
else
    printf 'Handover\nFiles: %s\n' "${#sources[@]}" > "$destination"
    for file in "${sources[@]}"; do
        printf 'Source: %s\n' "$file" >> "$destination"
        cat "$file" >> "$destination"
    done
    printf 'Saved: %s\n' "$destination"
fi

Positive-PID signals and explicit ps columns only. pgrep -x patterns allow ordinary names without regex characters; -u takes a modeled username. renice uses absolute values; ordinary-user priority limits are fixed. Exited entries are hidden from queries and children are adopted by synthetic init without a zombie/wait stage. Commands belong to this process terminal, not the separate script interpreter. Simulator notes label nonzero status; show is a simulator-only snapshot helper.

concepts.title: A parent and its child are separate processes
concepts.text: PPID points to the parent. Ending a parent does not automatically end its child. In this fixed model, a child whose parent ends is adopted by init and reports PPID 1; real systems may also have subreapers or a temporary zombie/wait stage, which are not modeled here.

concepts.title: Identify the whole family before changing it
concepts.text: Two workers can have the same name and owner but belong to different controllers. Record the PIDs belonging to the old controller before ending it, because the child’s displayed parent can change afterward. A name-only selection is not enough for this assignment.

concepts.title: A neighbor belongs to a local port
concepts.text: Directly connected devices use LLDP to share who they are and which port is connected (Link Layer Discovery Protocol). The receiving device keeps this information under its local port. Chassis ID identifies the sending device; port ID identifies its sending port. Names describe devices but are not these fixed identifiers. This information is not forwarded through another port.

concepts.title: One direction does not prove the other
concepts.text: Transmit and Receive are independent controls. A port with receive disabled can still send. Both devices and both local ports must be enabled and physically up for two-way learning. A current row also requires delivery to remain possible now.

concepts.title: Apply settings, then send explicitly
concepts.text: Applying the draft changes configuration but does not create or refresh neighbor records. Some configuration changes can remove old records. Send now transmits one advertisement from one selected local port using applied settings. Send from each side when both receiving inventories must be populated. This native simulation does not interpret IOS commands.

concepts.title: Cached time is simulated time
concepts.text: The sender advertises a lifetime (TTL) in seconds. Advance time ages the records but never sends for you. Exactly at the expiry timestamp the row disappears. CDP and automatic LLDP scheduling are not modeled.

concepts.title: Names and descriptions describe an identity
concepts.text: System name is advertised device-wide; port description belongs to the sending port. Changing either does not replace the fixed chassis/port identity. The receive-side cache may continue to display the previous text until another advertisement arrives.

concepts.title: The sender supplies the lifetime
concepts.text: A receiving port ages this sender using the TTL in the received advertisement, not its own device TTL. Updating the sender lifetime does not rewrite the old cached expiry. A new advertisement replaces the cached fields and refreshes the receive timestamp.

concepts.title: Current inventory requires refresh
concepts.text: This simulator marks a still-unexpired row historical when its recorded fields differ from the current sender or delivery no longer works. That simulator-only diagnostic is not a standard LLDP wire field. Apply metadata edits before sending from every affected local port.

concepts.title: A global edit can affect several neighbors
concepts.text: The same system name and lifetime are advertised on every transmitting port of the device. Refresh each attached receiver that the task names, and preserve unrelated port descriptions and peer settings.

concepts.text: Turning off Transmit on one port stops its advertisements without disabling Receive. The peer can still advertise toward this port. This is a discovery-information choice, not a data-traffic filter, authentication control or complete security policy.

concepts.title: A graceful stop removes the peer record
concepts.text: On a live link, this model sends a final TTL-zero withdrawal when an enabled transmitter is disabled. The attached receiver removes that sender record. Apply the transmit change, then inspect both receiving inventories.

concepts.title: Absence is not proof of correct policy
concepts.text: A cache can be empty because a receiver or physical link was disabled. This task also requires retained inbound discovery and the entire expected configuration, including link-up state, so those shortcuts fail.

concepts.title: Healthy work stays healthy

concepts.title: Attach a filesystem to a directory
concepts.text: A filesystem organizes stored data. Mounting attaches it at a directory called a mountpoint. Here the virtual volumes and directories are supplied, and every operation is simulated. There is no infrastructure to prepare.

concepts.title: Match the identity in the ticket
concepts.text: The ticket assigns each volume a purpose by UUID. blkid lists its current device name, UUID and filesystem type; it does not discover what a volume is used for. A /dev name may change. Copying the supplied lowercase UUID keeps the saved choice tied to that volume in this exercise.

concepts.title: Read one saved line
concepts.text: The file /etc/fstab holds saved mount instructions. Each line has six fields: source, mountpoint, type, options, dump frequency and check order. Match the type to the inventory. rw means writable, ro means read-only, and auto selects a fresh-session mount. defaults uses writable/automatic policy here. Keep the last two supplied numbers; this simulator performs no backup or filesystem check.

concepts.title: Save, mount, then verify
concepts.text: Type file changes in the editor and choose Save configuration. Validate configuration checks the saved file without mounting it. In the terminal, mount followed by a directory attaches its saved entry; mount alone lists current mounts. Test saved mounts tries independent copies with changed device names. It is not a real boot and cannot change your current session.

concepts.title: An access policy belongs to a mount
concepts.text: rw requests writable access and ro requests read-only access. This is separate from file ownership or permission bits: changing a saved mount policy is not a permission repair. The task checks both saved and current policies.

concepts.title: A saved edit does not change an existing mount
concepts.text: The saved file supplies future mount requests. A filesystem already mounted with ro stays ro after you save rw. Compare the editor, saved file and live table separately. An unsaved editor change has not even changed the saved instruction.

concepts.title: Apply the supported policy workflow

concepts.title: Turn printed output into a value
concepts.text: Command substitution, written $(command), runs a command and gives you its normal printed output as a value. labels=$(sort -u loans.txt) creates labels from that output. The file name is an input to sort; it is not the value stored in labels.

concepts.title: Keep the value together
concepts.text: Use double quotes when printing the stored value: printf '<%s>\n' "$labels". Otherwise spaces and line breaks can divide it into arguments, and wildcard text such as *.txt can select virtual filenames. The quoted value stays text.

concepts.title: Understand the end of the output
concepts.text: Capture removes line breaks at the end of command output. It keeps spaces and line breaks inside the value. sort normally finishes its last row with a line break; the closing > therefore follows the last captured row. Later lessons explore several final line breaks and command status.

labels=$(sort -u loans.txt)
printf 'Loan labels: <%s>\n' "$labels"

solution:
source=$1
destination=$2
if [ -z "$destination" ] || [ "$destination" = "$source" ]; then
    printf 'Invalid destination\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
if [ -f "$source" ]; then
    :
else
    printf 'Missing note: %s\n' "$source" >&2
    exit 2
fi
evidence=$(cat "$source")
printf 'Report: %s\nEvidence: <%s>\nEnd report\n' "$REPORT_TITLE" "$evidence" > "$destination"
printf 'Saved: %s\n' "$destination"

concepts.title: Remove ending line breaks, keep the evidence
concepts.text: $(cat "$source") reads command output into a value. Capture removes every line break at the end. It keeps line breaks at the start and inside, spaces, tabs and other text. An empty or all-line-break note becomes an empty value.

concepts.title: Quoting preserves what remains
concepts.text: Double quotes preserve the captured value, including an empty value. They cannot bring back ending line breaks that capture removed. Characters such as *, %, backslashes and $(...) printed by cat are data; the output is not executed again.

concepts.title: Print the report deliberately
concepts.text: Use %s for text values and explicit \n for the report's own line breaks. printf 'Evidence: <%s>\n' "$note" places > immediately after the remaining evidence. The optional input comparison makes invisible spaces and line breaks visible.

concepts.title: Recognize invisible characters
concepts.text: Here a line break means the newline character written \n in scripts and feedback. A tab is written \t. A carriage return, written \r, is another character and stays in captured text. These differences can appear in the input and output comparison.

concepts.title: Check before replacing a file
concepts.text: Validate the destination and source before using >. A missing source must preserve an existing report. The task lists the exact checks and error messages; opening an output file too early can destroy useful work.

%s

' 'Gallery  A' '100% ready')
printf 'Note: <%s>
' "$note"

teaching.prerequisite_note: Use helper functions, return and separate error output. A captured value and the command's status answer different questions.

concepts.title: Capture output and check status separately
concepts.text: An assignment such as reply=$(suggest_route) stores normal output. Its status is the captured command's status. Save it immediately with route_status=$?, or put the assignment in an if condition. A later printf has its own status and replaces $?; the stored reply does not tell you that status.

concepts.title: A nonzero result can carry useful information
concepts.text: The practice helper returns 4 and still prints a useful route. The assignment helper returns 0 for matching BLOCK: lines, 1 for no matches and 2 for its explicit missing-source check. Those are ordinary supported helper results, not simulator failures. Unsupported commands, limits and Stop are different: they leave the run ungraded.

concepts.title: Normal output and diagnostics stay separate
concepts.text: Capture collects normal output only. A helper's >&2 messages still appear in the error-output view. Keep those diagnostics separate from the Findings value. In this assignment, a hold is a useful report with status 1; a missing source has diagnostics and status 2, with no normal report.

concepts.title: Make a decision before reporting it
concepts.text: The starter prints Source before inspecting $?, so it inspects printf's status instead of the helper's. A successful helper is not automatically a ready decision: this helper uses 0 to mean that blocking text was found. Follow the stated mapping rather than guessing from an empty or nonempty value.

suggest_route() {

}

printf 'Reply: <%s>\nStatus: %s\n' "$reply" "$route_status"
teaching.inputs: No arguments, files or supplied variables. The example defines a small helper, captures its reply, and creates route_status. The outer printf succeeds even when the helper returned 4.

scenarios.explanation: The assignment-only command gets the captured helper's status. A later printf replaces $?, so the decision needs a saved status or immediate condition. The helper explicitly checks a missing source and returns 2; it does not rely on recovering a simulator failure. Nonzero hold/no-match statuses are useful results, while unsupported/limit/Stopped outcomes remain ungraded.

scenarios.title: Preview or publish a batch investigation safely
scenarios.summary: Combine intact captured output, reliable status, isolated variables and shared inspection files.
scenarios.objective:
Arguments are mode (preview or save), destination, then one or more source files; REPORT_TITLE is supplied. Build a report headed Review: TITLE and Decision: ready or hold. For each source argument, print Source: NAME followed by all lines containing literal BLOCK:, in argument order. Finish every report line with a line break. Any match means hold/status 1; otherwise ready/status 0. Keep the original title, literal text and repeated source arguments.

Append Checked: NAME and a line break to scan-ledger.txt for each source, keeping its existing text. Preview prints the report and preserves the destination; it still updates the ledger. Save replaces only the destination and prints Saved: DEST then Decision: VALUE, each on its own line. Leave every other file unchanged.

Check everything before any changes. Fewer than three arguments, unknown mode or empty destination gives Usage: preview|save DEST SOURCE... on error output. Next, destination scan-ledger.txt gives Unsafe destination. Then check sources in order: empty name gives Empty source name; destination collision gives Unsafe destination; scan-ledger.txt as source gives Unsafe source; missing source gives Missing source: NAME. Every guard failure prints only the stated message on error output, ends it with a line break, returns 2 and leaves all files unchanged. Use the supplied filenames exactly.

hints: The helper changes REPORT_TITLE and appends to the ledger. Check every source and collision before invoking it.
Call the existing helper inside capture, then save its result status immediately. The child's variable assignment stays inside, while its virtual file writes remain visible.

initial.source:
review_batch() {
    REPORT_TITLE='Working scan'
    blocked=0
    for source in "$@"; do
        printf 'Checked: %s\n' "$source" >> scan-ledger.txt
        printf 'Source: %s\n' "$source"
        if grep -F 'BLOCK:' "$source"; then blocked=1; fi
    done
    return "$blocked"
}

# Then create the requested preview or saved report using the original title.

solution:
review_batch() {
    REPORT_TITLE='Working scan'
    blocked=0
    for source in "$@"; do
        printf 'Checked: %s\n' "$source" >> scan-ledger.txt
        printf 'Source: %s\n' "$source"
        if grep -F 'BLOCK:' "$source"; then blocked=1; fi
    done
    return "$blocked"
}
if [ "$#" -lt 3 ]; then
    printf 'Usage: preview|save DEST SOURCE...\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
mode=$1
destination=$2
shift 2
if [ "$mode" != preview ] && [ "$mode" != save ]; then
    printf 'Usage: preview|save DEST SOURCE...\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
if [ -z "$destination" ]; then
    printf 'Usage: preview|save DEST SOURCE...\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
if [ "$destination" = scan-ledger.txt ]; then
    printf 'Unsafe destination\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
for source in "$@"; do
    if [ -z "$source" ]; then
        printf 'Empty source name\n' >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    if [ "$source" = "$destination" ]; then
        printf 'Unsafe destination\n' >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    if [ "$source" = scan-ledger.txt ]; then
        printf 'Unsafe source\n' >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    if [ -f "$source" ]; then
        :
    else
        printf 'Missing source: %s\n' "$source" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
done
body=$(review_batch "$@")
result=$?
if [ "$result" -eq 0 ]; then decision=ready; else decision=hold; fi
if [ "$mode" = preview ]; then
    printf 'Review: %s\nDecision: %s\n%s\n' "$REPORT_TITLE" "$decision" "$body"
else
    printf 'Review: %s\nDecision: %s\n%s\n' "$REPORT_TITLE" "$decision" "$body" > "$destination"
    printf 'Saved: %s\nDecision: %s\n' "$destination" "$decision"
fi
exit "$result"

teaching.prerequisite_note: Combine the first three capture tasks with safe batches and function scope. No arrays or arithmetic are required.

concepts.title: A called helper runs inside the capture
concepts.text: A function defined earlier is available inside $(helper arguments). Capture uses an isolated shell environment: the helper sees the caller's values, but its ordinary variable changes stay inside that capture. The parent still sees its original title afterward. This differs from calling an ordinary function directly, whose non-local assignments can change caller variables.

concepts.title: Files are still shared
concepts.text: An isolated variable environment does not isolate virtual files. The practice helper changes title inside the capture and appends to museum-ledger.txt. The outside title stays original, but the file view shows the new ledger line. Capturing a command is not a way to undo its file writes.

concepts.title: Validate the whole batch before a helper with effects
concepts.text: The assignment helper appends to scan-ledger.txt. Check every source and collision first, including a late missing source, before calling it. Preview preserves the destination, but it deliberately updates this inspection ledger. Failed validation must leave both report and ledger unchanged.

concepts.title: Keep the caller title and the batch decision
concepts.text: Capture the helper body, save its status before printing, and use the original supplied REPORT_TITLE in the wrapper. The helper returns 1 if any source contains BLOCK:, even if the last source is clear. Repeated source arguments remain separate inspections in the original order.

scenarios.explanation: A called function is inherited by the capture, with a child function-call frame. Its ordinary variable changes do not replace the parent's values. concepts.title: Two independent boundaries
concepts.text: A source-only list on SampleCore/archive out protects the store. An extended list on SampleEdge/clients in rejects only the listed TCP service toward the site. A source filter on the shared transit link would also affect the site, so placement matters.

concepts.title: Preserve the other service and direction
concepts.text: A TCP service deny must not accidentally block the same-numbered UDP check, the permitted destination, or independent reverse packets. No session is inferred: each displayed row is one explicit direction and protocol/port tuple.

concepts.title: Check the complete handover
concepts.text: Edit both router documents before Check configuration. All drafts apply together or none does. A blank document clears that router's modeled policy, not the other router. Every required allowed and denied row must pass from the same current network.

acl_teaching.example_description: SampleGuest must not reach SampleStore on TCP 8080/UDP 5353, while SampleStaff TCP 8080 works. Block both clients' TCP 2323 to SampleSite, keep its TCP 8443/UDP 2323 and the listed reverse packet working. Fill both documents, then Check example.

routers.SampleEdge:
ip access-list extended sample-site
 deny tcp any host 10.190.2.20 eq 2323
 permit ip any any
exit
interface clients
 ip access-group sample-site in
exit
routers.SampleCore:
ip access-list standard sample-store
 permit host 10.180.1.10
exit
interface archive
 ip access-group sample-store out
exit

try_change.description: After all checks pass, clear only SampleCore's document and Check example. The two store denials stop passing because SampleGuest now reaches it; the site service policy and all allowed checks remain correct. Refill/check both documents to repair.

concepts.title: Deleting a name is not deleting every owned file

concepts.title: Transfer only the requested report
concepts.text: chown USER:GROUP PATH changes one entry's numeric owner/group while retaining bytes and mode. Keep evidence untouched even when its owner name disappears. groupdel removes the unused group record; it is not a recursive file operation.

concepts.title: Inspect the final database and ownership

Remove wren's record and owned home only. The supplied outside evidence remains with its original numeric owner; the simulator does not model mail or running-process checks.
Remove the now-unused primary group after its user is gone. An existing account still using a primary group would prevent deletion.

concepts.title: Rename a team without changing its identity
concepts.text: groupmod -n NEW OLD changes a group's name, not its GID. Existing primary/supplementary memberships and file groups keep the number. Creating a different group is not equivalent to this team handover.

concepts.title: Expiry is a stored date here
concepts.text: usermod -e YYYY-MM-DD stores an account-expiry date; usermod -e '' USER clears it. This simulator grades the exact metadata only. It has no password database secrets, PAM, actual login or session to test, and clearing a date does not enable authentication.

concepts.title: Preserve the unaffected records and evidence
concepts.text: Combine the earlier creation, targeted chown and retirement tools. The obsolete supplementary group can be removed because nobody uses it as primary. Do not delete the renamed team: the successor needs its existing GID. Keep the historical archive's original numeric UID even after its user is removed.

Create the explicit successor from the supplied sample template. The previous onboarding lesson explains these flags; use the new team name after renaming it.
Record this exact UTC account-expiry date in local metadata. This exercise neither authenticates a login nor models password locking/PAM. An empty quoted date clears this field.
Transfer just the active handover report to the successor; keep the historical archive's numeric owner unchanged.
Remove the retiring account and its owned home after its active report is handed over. Outside historical data remains.
Remove the obsolete extra group. Its supplementary memberships disappear, while survivors' other group numbers stay the same.

Read the simulated shadow-style record: the account-expiry field stores a UTC day number. The ! sentinel is synthetic and contains no password/hash; other aging fields are empty. This query does not authenticate or establish that a login is allowed.

scenarios.title: Recover a branch identity and transit process
scenarios.summary: Separate an identity collision from a disabled transit process before touching interface settings.
scenarios.objective:
Branch cannot obtain a remote SPF candidate for Hub's 192.0.2.0/24 records network. Inspect router-level issues, give Branch an explicit nonzero router ID different from Transit and Hub, and enable Transit. Both supplied P2P attachments must become compatible.

Keep Transit's supplied process number, router ID and area, and keep Hub's whole process configuration unchanged. Preserve every supplied interface address, up state and OSPF port setting. Branch's local process number is not required to match its peers. Apply your edits and check current work.

Branch and Hub currently use the same router ID. Transit has a separate disabled-process issue.

concepts.title: What OSPF means here
concepts.text: Open Shortest Path First version 2 is an IPv4 link-state routing protocol. This workbench derives a compatible point-to-point graph and shortest-path candidates from configured fields. It does not observe a live adjacency or install a forwarding table.

concepts.title: Separate router and process identities
concepts.text: A router ID distinguishes a router; a process number identifies a local process. Different routers may use different process numbers. A duplicate router ID and a disabled process are different faults, and both need attention in this example.

concepts.title: Read the current evidence
concepts.text: Inspect router-level issues before changing interface timers. Enabling Library removes its disabled-process issue, while choosing a distinct Studio router ID removes the identity collision. A remote prefix still needs a complete compatible path.

concepts.title: Edit, apply, then check
concepts.text: Use the router fields for process enable and router ID. Fill the worked example to place its desired settings in the practice draft, then apply/check explicitly. Assignment and practice use separate networks; unfinished draft text invalidates a previous applied success.

ospf_teaching.example_description: Studio and Library share a router ID, and Library is disabled. Give Studio a distinct nonzero router ID, enable Library, and preserve all supplied interface settings. Studio should then have a remote candidate for Library's 172.16.41.0/24 shelves network. The worked path costs 5+4=9; Library's reverse interface cost 8 is not the outgoing Studio cost.

example_actions.explanation: Change only Studio's router ID to 101.0.0.9. Keep its enabled state, local process number and area.
Enable Library's process while retaining its router ID, local number and area. Then apply/check this separate practice draft.

try_change.description: After the worked repair, change Studio's router ID back to Library's 101.0.0.1, apply, and inspect the two failed behavior rows. Restore 101.0.0.9 to repair the example.

concepts.title: Area belongs to the local process
concepts.text: These single-area fixtures give each router one area field. Peers must agree on it. The number need not be zero in every independent example; the assignment explicitly asks for area 0. Local process numbers remain separate labels.

concepts.title: Two intervals, one compatibility decision
concepts.text: Hello is the configured interval between Hello messages in a real protocol; Dead is the configured time without hearing a peer before it is lost. Here their positive values are compared only. Both ends must match on each interval; no messages or missed-Hello clock are simulated.

concepts.title: Preserve the physical network
concepts.text: The supplied addresses and up flags stay unchanged. On supported P2P links, a mask difference is a diagnostic warning, not a Hello blocker. Repair the requested process/timer fields instead of renumbering an attachment.

concepts.title: Choose a coherent endpoint repair
concepts.text: Workshop uses area 5 and intervals 5/20; Depot uses area 3 and 10/40. The example moves Workshop to area 3 and 10/40. Matching Depot to Workshop's intervals would also restore timing compatibility after the area repair, without requiring equal process numbers.

ospf_teaching.example_description: Repair Workshop–Depot in area 3 and obtain a remote candidate for 172.17.42.0/24. Change Workshop's area and both timer fields, keeping all addresses/up flags, both local process numbers/router IDs and Depot's stock port unchanged. This example compares configured parameters; it does not demonstrate a stable live adjacency.

example_actions.explanation: Set Workshop's process area to 3, retaining its local process number, router ID and enabled state.
Set Workshop/depot Hello 10 and Dead 40 to match Depot/workshop. Retain cost 4 and active P2P operation, then apply/check.

try_change.description: After the worked repair, change only Workshop/depot Dead from 40 to 80 and apply. Its peer still has 40, so the compatibility and remote-route rows fail immediately in the snapshot. Restore 40 to repair.

scenarios.title: Restore two equal-cost first hops
scenarios.summary: Calculate outgoing transport plus destination-LAN cost without confusing the reverse direction.
scenarios.objective:
Ingress currently prefers only East for Storage's 198.51.100.0/24 records network. concepts.title: Read outgoing costs in the right direction
concepts.text: Each edge uses the sending router's interface cost. To reach a remote LAN, add each outgoing transport cost and the destination router's LAN cost. The opposite-direction interface values belong to a different calculation.

concepts.title: Equal-cost choices form a set
concepts.text: Equal-cost multipath, or ECMP, retains every shortest first-hop choice. Two compatible physical paths do not guarantee two route choices when their totals differ. This task checks the complete first-hop set, not one arbitrarily selected path or a packet load-balancing result.

concepts.title: Keep forward and reverse calculations separate

concepts.title: Choose values from the path equation

concepts.text: A passive OSPF interface can contribute its attached prefix while forming no OSPF peer there. Disabling OSPF removes that contribution instead. The required policy therefore needs both enabled and passive, with the supplied LAN parameters retained.

concepts.title: Read a supplied service unit
concepts.text:
A unit file tells the service manager how a named unit works. [Unit] holds its description and dependencies. [Service] describes how its program starts. A target is a named group of units to start together. [Install] tells Enable which target link to create; it does not start a program. The repaired separate example contains:

[Unit]
Description=App for sketch
[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/sim/bin/sketch-app
[Install]
WantedBy=sketch.target

Type=simple starts a program intended to keep running. ExecStart selects the program. The supplied /sim/bin identifiers name fixed virtual programs here; they are not host executables. Change the wrong ExecStart line, then save, reload the manager, and stop/start the old running service.

concepts.title: Saved files, loaded definitions and running programs
concepts.text: Saving changes a supplied file. Run systemctl daemon-reload to make the service manager read saved unit definitions; this does not restart a running program. A program already running keeps its previous settings until you stop and start it. A previous passing check or old log entry does not prove the current work is correct.

concepts.title: Investigate before changing more files
concepts.text: Use systemctl cat sketch-app.service to inspect its saved backing text and systemctl status sketch-app.service for current status. Open Loaded definition and current inputs below the editor to see the saved and loaded unit text and the settings used by its current program. systemctl show sketch-app.service -p Requires,Wants,After lists the supported dependency properties. journalctl -u sketch-app.service -o cat shows retained virtual messages. These queries change nothing; old messages are history, not proof of current success.

concepts.title: Start, then inspect status and logs
concepts.text: Here, starting a service also lets the simulated program initialize. A successful start message can still be followed by a configuration failure; inspect status and logs. A simple service is intended to keep running. Its active label alone does not prove the application is ready.

concepts.title: Current service and the next session
concepts.text: A target is a named group of units to start together. The default selects the group for the next session. Enabling links a service to that group; it does not start the program now. Stop affects the running program without removing that link. The default chooses the next-session target. Check work also tests the next session in a separate copy, so that check cannot repair the current assignment.

concepts.title: Saved files, loaded definitions and running programs
concepts.text: Saving changes a supplied file. Run systemctl daemon-reload to make the service manager read saved unit definitions; this does not restart a running program. A program already running keeps its previous settings until you stop and start it. A previous passing check or old log entry does not prove the current work is correct.

concepts.title: Investigate before changing more files
concepts.text: Use systemctl cat gallery-app.service to inspect its saved backing text and systemctl status gallery-app.service for current status. These queries change nothing; old messages are history, not proof of current success.

concepts.title: Optional failure is different from a required failure
concepts.text: Wants requests an optional unit while allowing the requesting start job to succeed if that unit fails. Requires together with After can block activation on a required failure. Neither dependency itself establishes readiness. Keep the actual optional failure visible rather than inventing a success or deleting the helper.

concepts.title: Start, then inspect status and logs
concepts.text: Here, starting a service also lets the simulated program initialize. A successful start message can still be followed by a configuration failure; inspect status and logs. A simple service is intended to keep running. Its active label alone does not prove the application is ready.

concepts.title: Current service and the next session
concepts.text: A target is a named group of units to start together. The default selects the group for the next session. Enabling links a service to that group; it does not start the program now. Stop affects the running program without removing that link. The default chooses the next-session target. Check work also tests the next session in a separate copy, so that check cannot repair the current assignment.

solution:
case "$1" in

        if test "$#" -ne 1; then
            printf 'Usage: card brief|full LABEL\n' >&2
            exit 2
        fi
        printf 'Usage: card brief|full LABEL\n'

        ;;
esac

concepts.title: Choose the first matching arm
concepts.text: case "$1" in starts a decision using the entire first argument. A pattern ends at ), its commands follow, and ;; finishes that arm. The first match wins; later arms do not run. End the decision with esac. Patterns separated by | choose the same commands, such as quick|summary).

concepts.text: Use *) as the final arm for everything else. Print a useful diagnostic to standard error and choose a nonzero exit status. Check help separately before ordinary argument counts when help has a different interface. No-match alone returns 0; it is not an error handler.

concepts.title: Patterns and values have different roles

In patterns, unquoted * matches any number of bytes and ? one byte; quoting either makes it literal. quick* is a broad pattern; 'quick*' expects a literal star. Use exact mode names here. When printing a label, quote it and use a fixed printf format.

concepts.title: Keep the workbench boundary clear
